content: \n								I kinda hope the team actually sees this review. This is *by far* the best iteration of the Two Point franchise so far, I am obsessed. The introduction of some of the new systems is just so good, like the expeditions, and how there are actually different levels of quality to exhibits, or that you have to piece together dino skeletons. It makes the game so much deeper to have to go on harder expeditions, or keep visiting places with better trained staff to get higher quality exhibits. You can make the entire museum and technically still have things to improve, or ways to grind forward into an even better production by replacing exhibits with higher quality versions - whereas, in the previous games once you made your "room" to handle an illness or teach a class you were somewhat done with that idea, unless you needed to build another one to handle bigger capacity. It was good, but it wasn't as deep or nuanced as the ideas in this game.Speaking of the "rooms" in the previous games, that exists somewhat in this game, but there's a nice mix of rooms and also exhibits that can go anywhere, so in terms of building out a space exactly how you want, you have waaay more freedom to be creative. If there's a Two Point Hospital 2 in the future, for instance, I would want to see this idea carried forward. Like, a nurses station doesn't have to be a room, it's an object manned by an employee.Also, there are lots of really nice quality of life improvements, like one-way doors, employee-only doors, etc. It's very helpful, and overdue.One other random thing that sort of blew my mind is, in the supernatural museum, you can catch poltergeists and turn them into an exhibit. But it's brilliantly implemented in both a thematic and gameplay sense, because the poltergeists will leave eventually once they're calmed down enough. Which means, sort of like above, you don't ever reach a perfect state of, like, I built that exhibit so I never need to touch it again. You will have to upkeep the exhibit in a gameplay sense yourself, and not purely by having another janitor or something. It's very good.

content: \n								After the past few years of hit-and-miss business sims I had convinced myself that the real heyday of tycoon games was back in the ‘90s, but Two Point Museum may have finally changed my mind.It's not a huge, revolutionary departure from Two Point Studios' recent run of quirky games, Hospital and Campus, but this time they've finally perfected the recipe. With its varied and challenging management layer, tons of cool props and exhibits to unlock, and a refreshingly dry sense of humor.I sometimes had a hard time dragging myself away from it.The thing that impresses me most about Two Point Museum compared to other recent games like Planet Coaster 2 is that it actually seems interested in challenging you to manage the finances of your operation as you’re building and decorating it.Maybe I’m a nerd, but that's at least half the reason I like these kinds of games. It's actually difficult to build a money printer that you can simply walk away from, but also not so punishing that I frequently got myself into big trouble that I couldn't wiggle my way out of. The balance, when it comes to juggling my balance sheets, feels just about… balanced.There are lots of useful tools to help you pull this off. The whole interface seems cleverly built to group relevant information together, and makes it really easy to quickly take action on common problems. The Pay Review screen for your staff is a great example. I can sort everyone in the museum by how satisfied or dissatisfied they are with their salary, then adjust it with a slider without having to even open up another menu. Then you get to watch their satisfaction change almost immediately, all from that screen. It's so effortless to navigate all of these complex considerations when so much thought has been put into how to organize it all in a way that makes my job more convenient.Whether I'm setting up a new exhibit or decorating the employee break room, everything is done in Two Point's whimsical, cartoony, almost claymation-like style. I might be displaying a fossil of a floppy disk or artifacts from a planet inhabited by cheese-loving aliens, but Museum leans into it all. Admittedly, I've never been particularly charmed by this schtick in previous Two Point games, and I'm still not. At least it's distinct and consistent. The PA announcements are often actually quite funny. "Bored guests are reminded that not everything has to be a party, okay?"Changing the focus from running a school or hospital to a museum does Two Point a lot of favors, though. When my goal is to impress my guests using elaborate displays, lots of little decorations, and floor plans that make sure they have to exit through the gift shop, I find myself zooming way down and paying a lot of attention to how everything might look at eye-level. On one of my favorite maps, I got to design a haunted house experience complete with cursed artifacts and, eventually, actual ghosts who can break out and cause mayhem if they don't get their weekly therapy appointment. So yeah, “simulation” is used a bit loosely here, and Two Point is all too happy to embrace goofiness over reality. It works!Each of the different museums has its own thematic and interesting challenges like this. In one, I was searching the seas for exotic fish to add to my wall-to-wall underwater wonderland. In another, I had to learn the mysterious symbology of an alien race to activate adjacency bonuses for my exhibits. What’s especially cool about that is the differences between each of these are so great that it's almost like you're getting multiple games in one.Two Point Aquarium, Two Point Planetarium, and Two Point Haunted Hotel. This kept things fresh and exciting well into my career – especially when my objectives started encouraging me to mix themes and disciplines from more than one area.Acquiring artifacts to show off and bring in crowds of gawkers involves unlocking and undertaking expeditions to everywhere from fossil-littered canyons to the far reaches of outer space. You have to manage the skills and traits of different staff members to unlock new ways of minimizing danger and maximizing rewards. It seems simple at first, but there's a lot of depth buried here.All of that harmonizes so well with the ways your staff can train and specialize at different tasks back home. An assistant who has a perk that allows them to move around quicker on the museum floor might also be able to remove a random event from an expedition that could cause injury or even "MIA" – functionally, death.There's a great progression from simpler, quicker, and lower-risk outings that bring back much less impressive attractions to long, deadly, and elaborate ones that can require several high-skill staff members and craftable items to tackle. The option to go for a Quick, Safe, or Detailed approach adds more strategy and nuance; increasing the survey level of a site also increases the chances of getting higher-rarity versions of your exhibits, and that presents a compelling reason to come back to places you've already been.This further ties into the satisfying unlock system, in which breaking down copies of exhibits you already have will increase your knowledge level for that exhibit and make your museum more educational. While general museum decorations are still unlocked with Kudosh, the achievement-based career currency making a return from Two Point Hospital and Campus, specifically themed decorations for a science or space museum only come from studying artifacts from that theme.Two Point Museum is a rewarding, deep, challenging, and highly entertaining tycoon game that demonstrates Two Point Studios has really hit its groove with this third iteration of the idea. The variety of different exhibits to unlock and level up, the thrill of discovering new expedition maps, and the array of clever and easy-to-use management tools make designing and running a museum joyful and consistently rewarding. Call the curator. They're really going to want to take a look at this.

It's actually difficult to build a money printer that you can simply walk away from, but also not so punishing that I frequently got myself into big trouble that I couldn't wiggle my way out of. The balance, when it comes to juggling my balance sheets, feels just about… balanced.There are lots of useful tools to help you pull this off. The whole interface seems cleverly built to group relevant information together, and makes it really easy to quickly take action on common problems. The Pay Review screen for your staff is a great example. I can sort everyone in the museum by how satisfied or dissatisfied they are with their salary, then adjust it with a slider without having to even open up another menu. Then you get to watch their satisfaction change almost immediately, all from that screen. It's so effortless to navigate all of these complex considerations when so much thought has been put into how to organize it all in a way that makes my job more convenient.Whether I'm setting up a new exhibit or decorating the employee break room, everything is done in Two Point's whimsical, cartoony, almost claymation-like style. I might be displaying a fossil of a floppy disk or artifacts from a planet inhabited by cheese-loving aliens, but Museum leans into it all. Admittedly, I've never been particularly charmed by this schtick in previous Two Point games, and I'm still not. At least it's distinct and consistent. The PA announcements are often actually quite funny. "Bored guests are reminded that not everything has to be a party, okay?"Changing the focus from running a school or hospital to a museum does Two Point a lot of favors, though. When my goal is to impress my guests using elaborate displays, lots of little decorations, and floor plans that make sure they have to exit through the gift shop, I find myself zooming way down and paying a lot of attention to how everything might look at eye-level. On one of my favorite maps, I got to design a haunted house experience complete with cursed artifacts and, eventually, actual ghosts who can break out and cause mayhem if they don't get their weekly therapy appointment. So yeah, “simulation” is used a bit loosely here, and Two Point is all too happy to embrace goofiness over reality. It works!Each of the different museums has its own thematic and interesting challenges like this. In one, I was searching the seas for exotic fish to add to my wall-to-wall underwater wonderland. In another, I had to learn the mysterious symbology of an alien race to activate adjacency bonuses for my exhibits. What’s especially cool about that is the differences between each of these are so great that it's almost like you're getting multiple games in one.Two Point Aquarium, Two Point Planetarium, and Two Point Haunted Hotel. This kept things fresh and exciting well into my career – especially when my objectives started encouraging me to mix themes and disciplines from more than one area.Acquiring artifacts to show off and bring in crowds of gawkers involves unlocking and undertaking expeditions to everywhere from fossil-littered canyons to the far reaches of outer space. You have to manage the skills and traits of different staff members to unlock new ways of minimizing danger and maximizing rewards. It seems simple at first, but there's a lot of depth buried here.All of that harmonizes so well with the ways your staff can train and specialize at different tasks back home. An assistant who has a perk that allows them to move around quicker on the museum floor might also be able to remove a random event from an expedition that could cause injury or even "MIA" – functionally, death.There's a great progression from simpler, quicker, and lower-risk outings that bring back much less impressive attractions to long, deadly, and elaborate ones that can require several high-skill staff members and craftable items to tackle. The option to go for a Quick, Safe, or Detailed approach adds more strategy and nuance; increasing the survey level of a site also increases the chances of getting higher-rarity versions of your exhibits, and that presents a compelling reason to come back to places you've already been.This further ties into the satisfying unlock system, in which breaking down copies of exhibits you already have will increase your knowledge level for that exhibit and make your museum more educational. While general museum decorations are still unlocked with Kudosh, the achievement-based career currency making a return from Two Point Hospital and Campus, specifically themed decorations for a science or space museum only come from studying artifacts from that theme.Two Point Museum is a rewarding, deep, challenging, and highly entertaining tycoon game that demonstrates Two Point Studios has really hit its groove with this third iteration of the idea. The variety of different exhibits to unlock and level up, the thrill of discovering new expedition maps, and the array of clever and easy-to-use management tools make designing and running a museum joyful and consistently rewarding. Call the curator. They're really going to want to take a look at this.

With its varied and challenging management layer, tons of cool props and exhibits to unlock, and a refreshingly dry sense of humor.I sometimes had a hard time dragging myself away from it.The thing that impresses me most about Two Point Museum compared to other recent games like Planet Coaster 2 is that it actually seems interested in challenging you to manage the finances of your operation as you’re building and decorating it.Maybe I’m a nerd, but that's at least half the reason I like these kinds of games. It's actually difficult to build a money printer that you can simply walk away from, but also not so punishing that I frequently got myself into big trouble that I couldn't wiggle my way out of. The balance, when it comes to juggling my balance sheets, feels just about… balanced.There are lots of useful tools to help you pull this off. The whole interface seems cleverly built to group relevant information together, and makes it really easy to quickly take action on common problems. The Pay Review screen for your staff is a great example. I can sort everyone in the museum by how satisfied or dissatisfied they are with their salary, then adjust it with a slider without having to even open up another menu. Then you get to watch their satisfaction change almost immediately, all from that screen. It's so effortless to navigate all of these complex considerations when so much thought has been put into how to organize it all in a way that makes my job more convenient.Whether I'm setting up a new exhibit or decorating the employee break room, everything is done in Two Point's whimsical, cartoony, almost claymation-like style. I might be displaying a fossil of a floppy disk or artifacts from a planet inhabited by cheese-loving aliens, but Museum leans into it all. Admittedly, I've never been particularly charmed by this schtick in previous Two Point games, and I'm still not. At least it's distinct and consistent. The PA announcements are often actually quite funny. "Bored guests are reminded that not everything has to be a party, okay?"Changing the focus from running a school or hospital to a museum does Two Point a lot of favors, though. When my goal is to impress my guests using elaborate displays, lots of little decorations, and floor plans that make sure they have to exit through the gift shop, I find myself zooming way down and paying a lot of attention to how everything might look at eye-level. On one of my favorite maps, I got to design a haunted house experience complete with cursed artifacts and, eventually, actual ghosts who can break out and cause mayhem if they don't get their weekly therapy appointment. So yeah, “simulation” is used a bit loosely here, and Two Point is all too happy to embrace goofiness over reality. It works!Each of the different museums has its own thematic and interesting challenges like this. In one, I was searching the seas for exotic fish to add to my wall-to-wall underwater wonderland. In another, I had to learn the mysterious symbology of an alien race to activate adjacency bonuses for my exhibits. An assistant who has a perk that allows them to move around quicker on the museum floor might also be able to remove a random event from an expedition that could cause injury or even "MIA" – functionally, death.There's a great progression from simpler, quicker, and lower-risk outings that bring back much less impressive attractions to long, deadly, and elaborate ones that can require several high-skill staff members and craftable items to tackle. The option to go for a Quick, Safe, or Detailed approach adds more strategy and nuance; increasing the survey level of a site also increases the chances of getting higher-rarity versions of your exhibits, and that presents a compelling reason to come back to places you've already been.This further ties into the satisfying unlock system, in which breaking down copies of exhibits you already have will increase your knowledge level for that exhibit and make your museum more educational. The variety of different exhibits to unlock and level up, the thrill of discovering new expedition maps, and the array of clever and easy-to-use management tools make designing and running a museum joyful and consistently rewarding. content: \n								After the past few years of hit-and-miss business sims I had convinced myself that the real heyday of tycoon games was back in the ‘90s, but Two Point Museum may have finally changed my mind.It's not a huge, revolutionary departure from Two Point Studios' recent run of quirky games, Hospital and Campus, but this time they've finally perfected the recipe. With its varied and challenging management layer, tons of cool props and exhibits to unlock, and a refreshingly dry sense of humor.I sometimes had a hard time dragging myself away from it.The thing that impresses me most about Two Point Museum compared to other recent games like Planet Coaster 2 is that it actually seems interested in challenging you to manage the finances of your operation as you’re building and decorating it.Maybe I’m a nerd, but that's at least half the reason I like these kinds of games. It's actually difficult to build a money printer that you can simply walk away from, but also not so punishing that I frequently got myself into big trouble that I couldn't wiggle my way out of. The balance, when it comes to juggling my balance sheets, feels just about… balanced.There are lots of useful tools to help you pull this off. The whole interface seems cleverly built to group relevant information together, and makes it really easy to quickly take action on common problems. The Pay Review screen for your staff is a great example. I can sort everyone in the museum by how satisfied or dissatisfied they are with their salary, then adjust it with a slider without having to even open up another menu. Then you get to watch their satisfaction change almost immediately, all from that screen. It's so effortless to navigate all of these complex considerations when so much thought has been put into how to organize it all in a way that makes my job more convenient.Whether I'm setting up a new exhibit or decorating the employee break room, everything is done in Two Point's whimsical, cartoony, almost claymation-like style. I might be displaying a fossil of a floppy disk or artifacts from a planet inhabited by cheese-loving aliens, but Museum leans into it all. Admittedly, I've never been particularly charmed by this schtick in previous Two Point games, and I'm still not. At least it's distinct and consistent. The PA announcements are often actually quite funny. "Bored guests are reminded that not everything has to be a party, okay?"Changing the focus from running a school or hospital to a museum does Two Point a lot of favors, though. When my goal is to impress my guests using elaborate displays, lots of little decorations, and floor plans that make sure they have to exit through the gift shop, I find myself zooming way down and paying a lot of attention to how everything might look at eye-level. On one of my favorite maps, I got to design a haunted house experience complete with cursed artifacts and, eventually, actual ghosts who can break out and cause mayhem if they don't get their weekly therapy appointment. So yeah, “simulation” is used a bit loosely here, and Two Point is all too happy to embrace goofiness over reality. It works!Each of the different museums has its own thematic and interesting challenges like this. In one, I was searching the seas for exotic fish to add to my wall-to-wall underwater wonderland. In another, I had to learn the mysterious symbology of an alien race to activate adjacency bonuses for my exhibits. What’s especially cool about that is the differences between each of these are so great that it's almost like you're getting multiple games in one.Two Point Aquarium, Two Point Planetarium, and Two Point Haunted Hotel. This kept things fresh and exciting well into my career – especially when my objectives started encouraging me to mix themes and disciplines from more than one area.Acquiring artifacts to show off and bring in crowds of gawkers involves unlocking and undertaking expeditions to everywhere from fossil-littered canyons to the far reaches of outer space. You have to manage the skills and traits of different staff members to unlock new ways of minimizing danger and maximizing rewards. It seems simple at first, but there's a lot of depth buried here.All of that harmonizes so well with the ways your staff can train and specialize at different tasks back home. An assistant who has a perk that allows them to move around quicker on the museum floor might also be able to remove a random event from an expedition that could cause injury or even "MIA" – functionally, death.There's a great progression from simpler, quicker, and lower-risk outings that bring back much less impressive attractions to long, deadly, and elaborate ones that can require several high-skill staff members and craftable items to tackle. The option to go for a Quick, Safe, or Detailed approach adds more strategy and nuance; increasing the survey level of a site also increases the chances of getting higher-rarity versions of your exhibits, and that presents a compelling reason to come back to places you've already been.This further ties into the satisfying unlock system, in which breaking down copies of exhibits you already have will increase your knowledge level for that exhibit and make your museum more educational. While general museum decorations are still unlocked with Kudosh, the achievement-based career currency making a return from Two Point Hospital and Campus, specifically themed decorations for a science or space museum only come from studying artifacts from that theme.Two Point Museum is a rewarding, deep, challenging, and highly entertaining tycoon game that demonstrates Two Point Studios has really hit its groove with this third iteration of the idea. The variety of different exhibits to unlock and level up, the thrill of discovering new expedition maps, and the array of clever and easy-to-use management tools make designing and running a museum joyful and consistently rewarding. content: \n								If you have played theme hospital (yes, I am that old) and then the two point hospital and two point campus games and you enjoyed those I'd suggest you will most likely love this game as well. Don't shoot me if you don't, I said most likely!This game does have a difference as you need to go explore to get exhibitions. Which is very important as you are running a museum.  Pro's:* I love the artwork and the detail* I love you have the campaign where you try to check all the objective boxes and a sandbox mode.* You can decorate a lot in this game and it does matter what kind of decorations you use. * You can customise a lot of objects by changing the colour (I haven't used it yet but then again I am lazy but it's a nice to have)* Music is chill as usual* Announcements are funny and are not constant otherwise it would have gotten annoying* Keyboard and mouse is easily usable and you can easily change keybinds if you want to change them* Game runs smoothly* Most exhibitions have different qualities. Which makes you want to explore more as you want the best one. * You have different outcomes while exploring if you do not have the right tools for the events which gives exploring another level than just mindlessly clicking explore.* Increasing knowledge needs you to explore as wellCons:* It is probably a bug but I tried using zones but have noticed that some workers are not really listening. Example: I put two botanists in a zone where there are plant exhibitions and they don't water them. So I hired one extra that was free to do whatever he liked and that one came to water the plants. Makes having zones a bit redundant. * Please give me an option to change the colour on "halve" a wall. Sometimes the wall colouring bugs out where I have to just delete it and place it again. (If there is a way and I haven't found it yet => do comment on this post)* I don't know if I missed the explanation but I did not know you could train the same skill multiple times. I mean you could to it in previous games but it was more noticeable there. So I only noticed way too late. And I know I am not the only one. Overall a fun and addictive game. I would recommend this game if this is the type of game you like. If you are doubting to buy it, give it a chance... You never know. Maybe you'll become an addict like me

content: \n								I went to go fire up Two Point Campus and found out this game was coming out. What a pleasant surprise. You'll sink many hours into this game. I end up falling in love with my creations and have to convince myself to move onto the next levels. I think that the expedition system is really cool and the humor is, once again, on point.My few criticisms would include:1. The partition wall tool is frustrating. Sometimes you simply cannot place a wall where you want it despite there not being any obstructions. When you load into the second map, there are 2 ticket kiosks placed inline with walls in a way where the employees access them from behind (think, like, when you check-in at the counter at the airport). Cool, indeed, but this is nearly impossible to replicate in a neat way. It would be awesome if the walls joined up to the edges of kiosks considering that the game clearly wants to showcase that.2. The game is too easy, especially if you played the other games in the series. The active pause makes it a breeze to address any serious problems the moment you're notified. If you're diligent and pay attention to the prompts, money is never an issue. 3. There's a bunch of wallpaper & flooring options, which is great. The issue is that there's only a small handful that look sleek and the result is that your museums end up looking highly similar despite the different themes. 4. I wish there was a simple "apply to all" or "apply to room" for flooring & wallpaper. 5. I think it's about time that Two Point allows you to build vertically. I just don't see why adding stair, escalator, and elevator options with camera tools that let you toggle between floors cannot be done. In this game, I think being able to have different floors to separate exhibition types and create intricate pathing for guests would add a lot of depth.

content: \n								To preface, I never could get into Two Point Hospital or Two Point Campus. They both felt more like a puzzle game than a management game. Build a room, add stuff to that room to progress the game, move onto the next room.  Two Point Museum feels like a proper Tycoon game! You can have a Dinosaur Exhibit next to a Future Exhibit in the same room for example. No longer are you restricted on what you can do "per room" and you can also design the layout of your museum to your hearts content. It feels way more like you're playing Zoo Tycoon or Roller Coaster Tycoon than the previous two games. I also love the new Expedition mechanic where it adds a sort of "light looting" element where you need to conduct expeditions to add new exhibits to your museum. It adds a level of randomness to the game and makes each new play-through different from the last. Also, each exhibit "type" is very different from each other. content: \n								In the brief intervals where I actually get to play it, I love this game. It's the same Two Point world I've come to love and know.  The humor is cute, the little children in their dino outfits are adorable. I mostly enjoy the game play loop, although certain aspects seem unbalanced at this time. The game punishes you for having too many staff while simultaneously making progression impossible without the acquisition of new staff. Staff level up soooo slowly. There's often not much to do but sit and watch the barest-bones staff you can get away with (so you can actually make $20 a month) keep the museum barely afloat and check to see if the one you need to have level up has managed it in the past half hour. I came here to play a management sim, not watch what often feels like a vaguely interactive movie. When there's actually stuff to manage and run it's very fun, but the game does not respect my time at all.The unforgivable thing is that it just keeps crashing. If I said this game had crashed 100 times in the 25 hours I've been playing (and I walked away a lot, I would say my play time is more like 15 hours) it I would be underselling just how grim the situation is. Moving the screen? Moving an object? There's a good chance the game is going to kick you back to the desktop. Think you can get around the hassle by quick-saving every couple of minutes? Yeah, that causes crashes too. I had been following a guide describing different ways you can attempt to fix the crashes which seemed to be yielding some results. I managed to keep the game open for five minutes at a time, then ten, and then it gave me the blue screen of death and sent my rig into a coma. When I managed to wake it half an hour later my save was corrupted. I suffered to get two stars on that aquarium and now it's gone, and my other less tedious museums with it. I'll be back when it's playable. I really hope that's soon.EDIT: I'm back, it is again playable! The devs helped me find which of my drivers was malfunctioning (turns out the app that was supposed to keep that updated had deleted itself) and even rescued my stupid aquarium (and all the less stupid museums too) from the depths of corruption hell. They were very kind about it and worked very quickly. I can get back to mulching pears in peace. Yay.

The humor is cute, the little children in their dino outfits are adorable. I mostly enjoy the game play loop, although certain aspects seem unbalanced at this time. The game punishes you for having too many staff while simultaneously making progression impossible without the acquisition of new staff. Staff level up soooo slowly. There's often not much to do but sit and watch the barest-bones staff you can get away with (so you can actually make $20 a month) keep the museum barely afloat and check to see if the one you need to have level up has managed it in the past half hour. I came here to play a management sim, not watch what often feels like a vaguely interactive movie. When there's actually stuff to manage and run it's very fun, but the game does not respect my time at all.The unforgivable thing is that it just keeps crashing. If I said this game had crashed 100 times in the 25 hours I've been playing (and I walked away a lot, I would say my play time is more like 15 hours) it I would be underselling just how grim the situation is. Moving the screen? Moving an object? There's a good chance the game is going to kick you back to the desktop. Think you can get around the hassle by quick-saving every couple of minutes? Yeah, that causes crashes too. I had been following a guide describing different ways you can attempt to fix the crashes which seemed to be yielding some results. I managed to keep the game open for five minutes at a time, then ten, and then it gave me the blue screen of death and sent my rig into a coma. When I managed to wake it half an hour later my save was corrupted. I suffered to get two stars on that aquarium and now it's gone, and my other less tedious museums with it. I'll be back when it's playable. I really hope that's soon.EDIT: I'm back, it is again playable! The devs helped me find which of my drivers was malfunctioning (turns out the app that was supposed to keep that updated had deleted itself) and even rescued my stupid aquarium (and all the less stupid museums too) from the depths of corruption hell. They were very kind about it and worked very quickly. I can get back to mulching pears in peace. Yay.

you can easily juggle multiple facets of design and management while still keeping your creative flair.The iterative process is fluid and the capabilities are obvious, with unexpected levels of intricacy.The various collections of items are extensive, the introduction of new mechanics is engaging.At several points I was streaming the game for a friend and found myself saying 'oh I wish it had X from Y',only to discover minutes later that it infact DOES have that mechanic and I simply hadn't reached it yet.The different exhibit types and the nature of their mechanical implementation are wildly varied,and after expecting 'dinosaur bones, but a science theme' I was constantly kept on my toes.Museums start out simple and effectively end up overlapping in fascinating ways.Experts in one field will inevitably be needed to help in others, so your museums might start out separatebut they'll inevitably merge into larger, mixed theme setups with huge overlaps and interactivity.The themes mesh together masterfully, some serious work went into making Space and Prehistory merge.I'd assumed I'd quickly find a favourite theme to focus on, and instead discovered I love the all equally.I ran into a few bugs during the early access period, and the developers have been nothing but helpful.Fast and transparent communication, offers to fix save files, day one mod support with guides.I'm looking forward to seeing more content and expansions, they can't come fast enough.Overall? Nine Cheesy Gubbins out of Nine.Classy and communicative developers, and a solid and addictive game at a ludicrously low price for 2025.A great starting point in the genre for anyone interested, and a must play for fans.

content: \n								As others have said, having played both Hospital and Campus, this is possibly the best Two Point game.  The same humor is throughout this game, so if you liked that before you'll be happy.  The expeditions add a very nice touch to the gameplay, having to assemble teams with the right qualifications to either enable possible good outcomes or prevent bad outcomes during the expedition.  As you do the expeditions, you can get better versions of the items you found, so there's a reason to keep going back once you've discovered each item form a certain expedition map.The museums themselves intertwine, so you bounce back and forth between them.  Although each has their specialty (like Prehistory, Water, or Supernatural), you can display artifacts from all themes in each museum.  In fact, this is encouraged as you will end up needing experts from multiple fields to do certain expeditions (like both a Water and Prehistory expert).The game itself walks you through the basics of the game through the campaign, so it doesn't throw too much at you at once.  This is good for newcomers to the series, but may seem klnd of slow to those who have been playing these types of games for awhile.  But then you always have sandbox mode you can play if that is the case.I have an older computer/graphics card (still Nvidia 1080 series) and have not had any issues playing so far.  So this game should work on nearly all systems.

You’ll go from displaying medieval torture devices and man eating plants to setting up interactive alien encounters, all while trying to prevent your visitors from getting too hands-on with history.Verdict: A Must-Play for Sim Fans and Chaos EnthusiastsWhether you’re a longtime fan of Two Point games or a newcomer looking for a hilarious management sim, Two Point Museum is an absolute gem. Two Point Museum isn’t just a game; it’s a madcap expedition through time, space, and the ridiculous inner workings of curating artifacts; some cursed, while barely keeping your museum from burning down (sometimes literally).The Announcer: Now 300% FunnierIf you thought the hospital and university announcer were hilarious, buckle up. This one’s got the comedic timing of a stand-up legend trapped in a PA system. From snarky remarks about totally ethical artifact acquisitions to sarcastic weather reports that have absolutely no bearing on museum operations, every announcement is gold. I found myself laughing and excited to hear what nonsense they’d come up with next.Expeditions: Because Buying Artifacts is for AmateursForget bidding at auctions like some regular, law-abiding museum curator. In Two Point Museum, you send people on wild adventures to uncover history’s lost treasures. Want a dinosaur fossil? Dispatch an underpaid team to the wilds! Need an ancient statue? Then send your team to a temple that may or may not be cursed! These expeditions are not only absurdly fun, but they also add a whole new layer of strategy—you’re constantly juggling your best explorers, their skills, and the ever-present risk of, well… "misplacing" a few staff members along the way.More Two Point Shenanigans, But BetterAt its core, this is the classic Two Point charm—wacky animations, beautifully chaotic management, and a steady stream of disasters that make every playthrough unique. The visual style is as polished and delightful as ever, and the sheer variety of exhibits keeps things fresh. You’ll go from displaying medieval torture devices and man eating plants to setting up interactive alien encounters, all while trying to prevent your visitors from getting too hands-on with history.Verdict: A Must-Play for Sim Fans and Chaos EnthusiastsWhether you’re a longtime fan of Two Point games or a newcomer looking for a hilarious management sim, Two Point Museum is an absolute gem. It’s clever, chaotic, and packed with enough humour to keep you laughing through every failed expedition and poorly placed dinosaur skeleton.Final Score: 9.8/10 – Funniest museum management sim of all time. Also, possibly the only one. But still.

content: \n								DAY1 DLC. Forced online for a singleplayer game. Can't play on handheld on trips. 270/1100 present reviews are non-steam purchases. Totally organic reviews /sWhat do you think happens when companies exploit past goodwill, shaft consumers for quick money and deliver poor quality products? Consumers conclude never to do business with them again and write spite reviews like this. I will refund this purchase after I'm done with review. I at least I hoped things would improve and I won't have to refund but on quick glance this has practically the same problems as TPC like ugly matte UI from TPC and game has unoptimized performance and liliput feel like TPC.  TPH and theme hospital remains the only good games in the franchise. 2K and Firaxis needs to learn buying PR influencers for Civ7 like Sega has done for TPM launch. This engine is now an assembly line to manufacture slop every 2-3years.Game development has stopped for TPC in 2years for good, tp encourage buying TPMuseum. Full TPCampus ended with 1/4th worth of content of that of TPHospital. Unacceptable as costs are same as TPH. TPM will likely be the same. I could be wrong but singer behind Jasmine Odyssey is still shafted and her voice reused, as I did not come across any songs new bits from her while playing. Meanwhile the annoying and unfunny lady radio host introduced in TPC is back and still just monotonous and boring as ever.Anyhow, below are excerpts from my TPC review, which incidentally looks applicable here too. But my point is to explain why I am not supporting this franchise: The bgm is even more generic now like some mobile mtx game.What a waste of money TPC was for me. Should have expected it from a typical Japanese company SEGA publisher adept at fleecing people. On top of that Denuvo crap making me fall for this scam of a game TPC has ensured I will never play another Two Point game again. With Denuvo you simply can't play offline when on trips or travelling. IT still TANKS performance no matter what access media wants to make you believe. I have both Steamdeck and ROG Ally.  Guess which one has better performance here. More powerful Ally? Nah, it's the Linux Steamdeck with no Denuvvo. Someone with either handheld can probably dual boot Windows/Bazzite and see the significant performance difference themselves.TPC was massive downgrade from Two Point Hospital and Theme Hospital. The "soul" from the humor was missing. It was just frustratingly boring. The artstyle and color choices are visibly jarring and old looking with a weird matte and velvet texture everywhere. Has a weird Mexican sweaty sepia tinge everywhere. The newly introduced radio host voiceactress is deeply unfunny going over and over on baguettes. I had to mute and play afterwards. While Jasmine Odyssey's real singer(Sophia?) is shafted and her lines reused from TPH.The gameplay wasn't at all fun. All the rooms were huge compared to TPH for some reason and so I have to zoom out, at which point the characters looked like little tardigrades crawling around. WORST OF ALL, when you were economically stable you had to do nothing but watch things go like 2000s god game crapwares from Peter Moleyneux. The game was terribly annoying to turn a profit early game with obfuscated mechanics(law of 8). Even after hours of play I don't get when a student does assignments and when not. TPH was far sensible you diagnose GP loop around then treatment. Because of the huge rooms, you were kinda always forced to expand and uglify the map. The gfx engine was horribly optimized vs hospital as well. The switch version I heard was unplayable from day1 and even for steam versions bugs got rarely fixed by devs if at all. And all these low quality effort was hidden behind thanks to Denuvvo, you know why, hiding bad development and ensuring game can't be refunded by the time one realizes.. This is coming from someone who loved TPH to bits enough to buy it with pocket money, after  playing all maps, out of support, and never touched it again(it's not bad but not a fan of replaying games without variance). Niche games shouldn't alienate their niche faithful base with cashgrabs and low effort. I thoroughly regretted buying TPC even at sale with the repetitive DLCs. Totally organic reviews /sWhat do you think happens when companies exploit past goodwill, shaft consumers for quick money and deliver poor quality products? Consumers conclude never to do business with them again and write spite reviews like this. I will refund this purchase after I'm done with review. I at least I hoped things would improve and I won't have to refund but on quick glance this has practically the same problems as TPC like ugly matte UI from TPC and game has unoptimized performance and liliput feel like TPC.  TPH and theme hospital remains the only good games in the franchise. 2K and Firaxis needs to learn buying PR influencers for Civ7 like Sega has done for TPM launch. This engine is now an assembly line to manufacture slop every 2-3years.Game development has stopped for TPC in 2years for good, tp encourage buying TPMuseum. Full TPCampus ended with 1/4th worth of content of that of TPHospital. Unacceptable as costs are same as TPH. TPM will likely be the same. I could be wrong but singer behind Jasmine Odyssey is still shafted and her voice reused, as I did not come across any songs new bits from her while playing. Meanwhile the annoying and unfunny lady radio host introduced in TPC is back and still just monotonous and boring as ever.Anyhow, below are excerpts from my TPC review, which incidentally looks applicable here too. But my point is to explain why I am not supporting this franchise: The bgm is even more generic now like some mobile mtx game.What a waste of money TPC was for me. Should have expected it from a typical Japanese company SEGA publisher adept at fleecing people. On top of that Denuvo crap making me fall for this scam of a game TPC has ensured I will never play another Two Point game again. With Denuvo you simply can't play offline when on trips or travelling. IT still TANKS performance no matter what access media wants to make you believe. I have both Steamdeck and ROG Ally.  Guess which one has better performance here. More powerful Ally? Nah, it's the Linux Steamdeck with no Denuvvo. Someone with either handheld can probably dual boot Windows/Bazzite and see the significant performance difference themselves.TPC was massive downgrade from Two Point Hospital and Theme Hospital. The "soul" from the humor was missing. It was just frustratingly boring. The artstyle and color choices are visibly jarring and old looking with a weird matte and velvet texture everywhere. Has a weird Mexican sweaty sepia tinge everywhere. The newly introduced radio host voiceactress is deeply unfunny going over and over on baguettes. I had to mute and play afterwards. While Jasmine Odyssey's real singer(Sophia?) is shafted and her lines reused from TPH.The gameplay wasn't at all fun. All the rooms were huge compared to TPH for some reason and so I have to zoom out, at which point the characters looked like little tardigrades crawling around. WORST OF ALL, when you were economically stable you had to do nothing but watch things go like 2000s god game crapwares from Peter Moleyneux. The game was terribly annoying to turn a profit early game with obfuscated mechanics(law of 8). Even after hours of play I don't get when a student does assignments and when not. TPH was far sensible you diagnose GP loop around then treatment. Because of the huge rooms, you were kinda always forced to expand and uglify the map. The gfx engine was horribly optimized vs hospital as well. The switch version I heard was unplayable from day1 and even for steam versions bugs got rarely fixed by devs if at all. And all these low quality effort was hidden behind thanks to Denuvvo, you know why, hiding bad development and ensuring game can't be refunded by the time one realizes.. This is coming from someone who loved TPH to bits enough to buy it with pocket money, after  playing all maps, out of support, and never touched it again(it's not bad but not a fan of replaying games without variance). Niche games shouldn't alienate their niche faithful base with cashgrabs and low effort. I thoroughly regretted buying TPC even at sale with the repetitive DLCs. I will probably buy TPM again when on sale since TPC has been only one failure yet in my eyes. But if TPM also follows TPC then I will abandon the series for good. Now Steam doesn't even allow me to post review if denuvvo is spelled correctly more than three times, wow Gabe

content: \n								DAY1 DLC. Forced online for a singleplayer game. Can't play on handheld on trips. 270/1100 present reviews are non-steam purchases. Totally organic reviews /sWhat do you think happens when companies exploit past goodwill, shaft consumers for quick money and deliver poor quality products? Consumers conclude never to do business with them again and write spite reviews like this. I will refund this purchase after I'm done with review. I at least I hoped things would improve and I won't have to refund but on quick glance this has practically the same problems as TPC like ugly matte UI from TPC and game has unoptimized performance and liliput feel like TPC.  TPH and theme hospital remains the only good games in the franchise. 2K and Firaxis needs to learn buying PR influencers for Civ7 like Sega has done for TPM launch. This engine is now an assembly line to manufacture slop every 2-3years.Game development has stopped for TPC in 2years for good, tp encourage buying TPMuseum. Full TPCampus ended with 1/4th worth of content of that of TPHospital. Unacceptable as costs are same as TPH. TPM will likely be the same. I could be wrong but singer behind Jasmine Odyssey is still shafted and her voice reused, as I did not come across any songs new bits from her while playing. Meanwhile the annoying and unfunny lady radio host introduced in TPC is back and still just monotonous and boring as ever.Anyhow, below are excerpts from my TPC review, which incidentally looks applicable here too. But my point is to explain why I am not supporting this franchise: The bgm is even more generic now like some mobile mtx game.What a waste of money TPC was for me. Should have expected it from a typical Japanese company SEGA publisher adept at fleecing people. On top of that Denuvo crap making me fall for this scam of a game TPC has ensured I will never play another Two Point game again. With Denuvo you simply can't play offline when on trips or travelling. IT still TANKS performance no matter what access media wants to make you believe. I have both Steamdeck and ROG Ally.  Guess which one has better performance here. More powerful Ally? Nah, it's the Linux Steamdeck with no Denuvvo. Someone with either handheld can probably dual boot Windows/Bazzite and see the significant performance difference themselves.TPC was massive downgrade from Two Point Hospital and Theme Hospital. The "soul" from the humor was missing. It was just frustratingly boring. The artstyle and color choices are visibly jarring and old looking with a weird matte and velvet texture everywhere. Has a weird Mexican sweaty sepia tinge everywhere. The newly introduced radio host voiceactress is deeply unfunny going over and over on baguettes. I had to mute and play afterwards. While Jasmine Odyssey's real singer(Sophia?) is shafted and her lines reused from TPH.The gameplay wasn't at all fun. All the rooms were huge compared to TPH for some reason and so I have to zoom out, at which point the characters looked like little tardigrades crawling around. WORST OF ALL, when you were economically stable you had to do nothing but watch things go like 2000s god game crapwares from Peter Moleyneux. The game was terribly annoying to turn a profit early game with obfuscated mechanics(law of 8). Even after hours of play I don't get when a student does assignments and when not. TPH was far sensible you diagnose GP loop around then treatment. Because of the huge rooms, you were kinda always forced to expand and uglify the map. The gfx engine was horribly optimized vs hospital as well. The switch version I heard was unplayable from day1 and even for steam versions bugs got rarely fixed by devs if at all. And all these low quality effort was hidden behind thanks to Denuvvo, you know why, hiding bad development and ensuring game can't be refunded by the time one realizes.. This is coming from someone who loved TPH to bits enough to buy it with pocket money, after  playing all maps, out of support, and never touched it again(it's not bad but not a fan of replaying games without variance). Niche games shouldn't alienate their niche faithful base with cashgrabs and low effort. I thoroughly regretted buying TPC even at sale with the repetitive DLCs. I will probably buy TPM again when on sale since TPC has been only one failure yet in my eyes. But if TPM also follows TPC then I will abandon the series for good. Now Steam doesn't even allow me to post review if denuvvo is spelled correctly more than three times, wow Gabe

content: \n								DAY1 DLC. Forced online for a singleplayer game. Can't play on handheld on trips. 270/1100 present reviews are non-steam purchases. Totally organic reviews /sWhat do you think happens when companies exploit past goodwill, shaft consumers for quick money and deliver poor quality products? Consumers conclude never to do business with them again and write spite reviews like this. I will refund this purchase after I'm done with review. I at least I hoped things would improve and I won't have to refund but on quick glance this has practically the same problems as TPC like ugly matte UI from TPC and game has unoptimized performance and liliput feel like TPC.  TPH and theme hospital remains the only good games in the franchise. 2K and Firaxis needs to learn buying PR influencers for Civ7 like Sega has done for TPM launch. This engine is now an assembly line to manufacture slop every 2-3years.Game development has stopped for TPC in 2years for good, tp encourage buying TPMuseum. Full TPCampus ended with 1/4th worth of content of that of TPHospital. Unacceptable as costs are same as TPH. TPM will likely be the same. I could be wrong but singer behind Jasmine Odyssey is still shafted and her voice reused, as I did not come across any songs new bits from her while playing. Meanwhile the annoying and unfunny lady radio host introduced in TPC is back and still just monotonous and boring as ever.Anyhow, below are excerpts from my TPC review, which incidentally looks applicable here too. But my point is to explain why I am not supporting this franchise: The bgm is even more generic now like some mobile mtx game.What a waste of money TPC was for me. Should have expected it from a typical Japanese company SEGA publisher adept at fleecing people. On top of that Denuvo crap making me fall for this scam of a game TPC has ensured I will never play another Two Point game again. With Denuvo you simply can't play offline when on trips or travelling. IT still TANKS performance no matter what access media wants to make you believe. I have both Steamdeck and ROG Ally.  Guess which one has better performance here. More powerful Ally? Nah, it's the Linux Steamdeck with no Denuvvo. Someone with either handheld can probably dual boot Windows/Bazzite and see the significant performance difference themselves.TPC was massive downgrade from Two Point Hospital and Theme Hospital. The "soul" from the humor was missing. It was just frustratingly boring. The artstyle and color choices are visibly jarring and old looking with a weird matte and velvet texture everywhere. Has a weird Mexican sweaty sepia tinge everywhere. The newly introduced radio host voiceactress is deeply unfunny going over and over on baguettes. I had to mute and play afterwards. While Jasmine Odyssey's real singer(Sophia?) is shafted and her lines reused from TPH.The gameplay wasn't at all fun. All the rooms were huge compared to TPH for some reason and so I have to zoom out, at which point the characters looked like little tardigrades crawling around. WORST OF ALL, when you were economically stable you had to do nothing but watch things go like 2000s god game crapwares from Peter Moleyneux. The game was terribly annoying to turn a profit early game with obfuscated mechanics(law of 8). Even after hours of play I don't get when a student does assignments and when not. TPH was far sensible you diagnose GP loop around then treatment. Because of the huge rooms, you were kinda always forced to expand and uglify the map. The gfx engine was horribly optimized vs hospital as well. The switch version I heard was unplayable from day1 and even for steam versions bugs got rarely fixed by devs if at all. And all these low quality effort was hidden behind thanks to Denuvvo, you know why, hiding bad development and ensuring game can't be refunded by the time one realizes.. This is coming from someone who loved TPH to bits enough to buy it with pocket money, after  playing all maps, out of support, and never touched it again(it's not bad but not a fan of replaying games without variance). Niche games shouldn't alienate their niche faithful base with cashgrabs and low effort. I thoroughly regretted buying TPC even at sale with the repetitive DLCs. I will probably buy TPM again when on sale since TPC has been only one failure yet in my eyes. But if TPM also follows TPC then I will abandon the series for good. content: \n Two Point Museum Review – Where Chaos and Culture CollideAnother absolute banger from the beautiful chaos factory that is Two Point Studios! If you’ve ever accidentally built a hospital with zero toilets or a university where the janitors were the real MVPs, you’ll feel right at home here — only now you’re the proud curator of a museum where priceless artifacts coexist with absolute nonsense (and somehow, it works).I sank 7 hours straight on release day — no breaks, just vibes and caffeine — and let me tell you, zero regrets. It’s that perfect blend of “I am a master strategist” and “why is my entire staff on break during a dinosaur fossil unveiling??” Keeps you on your toes in the best way.Performance check: My trusty GTX 1060 handles it like a champ — 1440p at 120fps on max settings without breaking a sweat. The classic Two Point charm is alive and well — goofy staff animations, guests who wander around like they misplaced their brains, and just enough weirdness to make you zoom in and lose 10 minutes watching your staff aggressively clean imaginary dust off a Alien exhibit.It’s rare for me to say this, but I genuinely would’ve paid more for this game. Absolute win. Buy it, build it, and prepare for chaos — because history has never been this hilariously unhinged.

The mortals you summon and trap are simpleminded creatures who are oblivious to the fact that they are trapped within the museum grounds. You can summon various objects within your museum grounds, including entire buildings, by simply using money. They don't need to be built, they just pop into existence.The mortals do not sleep, they barely eat or drink. Sometimes they have to sit down, and occasionally have a bread-stick, doughnut, sandwich, cup of coffee, bag of junk food, or a soda, but mostly they just work.Not attending their minimal needs weakens your hold on them. If your hold becomes too weak, they can break free of it, become self aware, and escape the museum. Visitors are somehow immune to your grasp as you cannot grab them or coerce them in any way. I normally never raise the price on a game, but there is a huge amount of variety, and when you think you have seen it all, you are not even close. Make sure you get to at least 3 stars and the game will open up even more for you! So excited to see what more there is to do and play. My museums are getting better, the layouts are improving, I am using all the various tile options, and wallpapers. This game rewards you with the effort you put in. If you like games like this, buy it. This to me deserves to be considered one of the greats, that will earn it's place in history, as an incredible game. I can't believe I was wondering if $29 dollars was worth the price. It's worth more!!! Buy it if you like this stuff and dedicate some time. The math is easy to meet, but choosing your layout is where the fun is. Take time making something that looks good, and just don't cram everything together to hit the check marks, you will be rewarded with an awesome looking museum, something you can be proud of.Know that you can always travel to different maps to add new exhibits to your museum that you have unlocked. I also feel like they have ramped up the management aspect in a way that makes it feel engaging and allows you to problem solve without being overwhelming or intrusive. content: \n								the game is very good. its good in the same way anno is good in that its a pleasant experience to look at and engage with everything. money management is relevant, which is more than you can say about most sims. the game is very wide and has decent amount of depth. its also very good at sustaining your focus. i only have 1 complaint with the gameplay and a few very minor complaints on the ux/systems level.my only real complaint is that the gachafication of the game is a bit too strong. you take on explorations get exhibits, which is great. but this game has a pretty excessive upgrade grind, similar to most other modern games especially survival crafting games: you level up the location of your exploration to get higher level exhibits, you break down exhibits to increase knowledge for those exhibits and get perk points. the 'end goal' is to get yellow level "pristine" (so legendary) exhibits and have maximum knowledge on exhibits. some exhibits also can have conditionals to be coupled with other exhibits of a certain subtype, which additionally explodes the repeat exploration requirement. its all a bit much and just artificially pads out game time by adding a level grind/loot box mechanic.minor complaints are: youre forced to replace exhibits with higher level exhibits while progressing, this will reset your museum tours that visit that exhibit. the pathing on tours breaks easily. your employees have perks that make them better for certain tasks but the game doesnt prioritize skilled employees from unskilled employees. basically, if you have someone with the tour perk giving a tour and they go on break, someone else will take their place and not relinquish it anymore. new rooms are forced to be built to functional completion, which adds some extra steps when designing layouts (finish room, go back into edit). everything else are even minor complaints and not even worth mentioning.so in short the game is joyous and fun, its good at directing and keeping your focus and lastly quite grindy. you definitely cant go wrong, if youre looking for a lightweight sim game. also its 30 bucks. support their decision to sell it for 30.

content: \n								Another triumph of the Two Point series. I adore this franchise and cannot recommend it enough for its humor and excellent game mechanics.I wasn't immediately sold on the Museum theme when they announced it, but pre-ordered because (aside from one DLC) I've never been disappointed by these developers. I was worried that it would feel like just the decorating parts of Campus and Hospital. As soon as I got to play it, I was sold.There are a lot of cool things happening here. With the Marine Life exhibits, you get a little taste of what Two Point Aquarium or Two Point Zoo would feel like as a game, for example. They've done a clever thing in this entry by having you get a 1 star museum, then forcing you to change to a different location to get a second 1 star museum before going back to the first location to raise to 2 stars. This gives you a lot of chance to learn from your design mistakes along the way and unlock more rooms before coming back to a previous museum to implement your new ideas. It makes you feel a lot more like you're curating all the museums at once, rather than just playing through themed levels. I just hit the point where I decided I needed to break down my entire museum layout and start over. They gave you a lot of useful tools for this process by letting you drag select an area to dismantle everything in it at once, rather than needing to sell//move each item individually. Being able to build freestanding walls is wildly useful for directing traffic - I just wish we had one-way turn styles or something similar to force guests to walk through a certain direction. Or could force guests to exit through the gift shop, for example.Are there a few launch issues? Sure. The most obnoxious right now is constantly being told you need more janitors, but they've already said they're looking at the issue and plan to dial that warning down. I think all the kinks will get worked out in the next few weeks and hopefully we'll get more tools in the coming months.I cannot wait to progress deeper into this campaign and keep expanding my museum empire. I can't wait to see what they have in mind for DLCs. I usually tell people to wait for games to be on sale before they pick them up. For this entry, I'd recommend it at the full price of admission.

content: \n								Another triumph of the Two Point series. I adore this franchise and cannot recommend it enough for its humor and excellent game mechanics.I wasn't immediately sold on the Museum theme when they announced it, but pre-ordered because (aside from one DLC) I've never been disappointed by these developers. I was worried that it would feel like just the decorating parts of Campus and Hospital. As soon as I got to play it, I was sold.There are a lot of cool things happening here. With the Marine Life exhibits, you get a little taste of what Two Point Aquarium or Two Point Zoo would feel like as a game, for example. They've done a clever thing in this entry by having you get a 1 star museum, then forcing you to change to a different location to get a second 1 star museum before going back to the first location to raise to 2 stars. This gives you a lot of chance to learn from your design mistakes along the way and unlock more rooms before coming back to a previous museum to implement your new ideas. It makes you feel a lot more like you're curating all the museums at once, rather than just playing through themed levels. I just hit the point where I decided I needed to break down my entire museum layout and start over. They gave you a lot of useful tools for this process by letting you drag select an area to dismantle everything in it at once, rather than needing to sell//move each item individually. Being able to build freestanding walls is wildly useful for directing traffic - I just wish we had one-way turn styles or something similar to force guests to walk through a certain direction. Or could force guests to exit through the gift shop, for example.Are there a few launch issues? Sure. The most obnoxious right now is constantly being told you need more janitors, but they've already said they're looking at the issue and plan to dial that warning down. I think all the kinks will get worked out in the next few weeks and hopefully we'll get more tools in the coming months.I cannot wait to progress deeper into this campaign and keep expanding my museum empire. I can't wait to see what they have in mind for DLCs. I usually tell people to wait for games to be on sale before they pick them up. For this entry, I'd recommend it at the full price of admission.

content: \n								I'm a massive fan of Two Point Studios games, and with Two Point Museum, they've truly exceeded all my expectations! From the very first moment, I was hooked on managing my own museum, and I haven't been able to put it down since.What I love most about this game is the sheer variety of museums you can build. Staff ignore the assigned zones and wander aimlessly, causing inefficiency and delays.Distracted Security: The police officers sometimes struggle to detect thieves, even when they're stealing in plain sight. This results in frequent thefts and frustrating losses of valuable exhibits.These issues, while not game-breaking, can significantly impact the gameplay experience. I hope Two Point Studios takes note and releases updates to fix these errors as soon as possible.In summary, Two Point Museum is a must-have game for any fan of management games. It has provided me with hours and hours of fun, and I'm sure I'll keep playing for a long time. If you like games with humour, challenges, and a big dose of creativity, you can't miss it!My personal rating:Gameplay: 9/10 (one point off for the bugs)Graphics: 9/10Sound: 10/10Fun: 10/10Recommendation: A must-buy! content: \n								I was fully aware as soon as this game was announced that I was going to be eaten alive by it, and it somehow exceeded my expectations. The different museums are fun and varied and it's set up so you move between them regularly as opposed to getting 3 stars and moving on, as it was in previous Two Point games. I feel like this structure works really well and keeps things fresh. It keeps you on your toes instead of staring at the screen in a semi-zombie state, waiting for your facility to meet the criteria to earn more stars. The game play loop is SO satisfying and casually addictive, I was iffy about having to run expeditions but I actually love that aspect the most. Playing it even has me wanting to take a second look at Campus, which I originally thought was a bit too different from Hospital for me to get into, but Museum seems to bridge that gap. If you're a fan of the studio's other games, this is definitely the best incarnation so far.

content: \n								I paid the extra $10 for the early release of this game and after playing for 5 days I can attest that this game is damn near perfect.  I honestly cannot think of one complaint so far. For those of you that have played other Two Point games, much of this game is similar but they added some excellent new features.The most important metric in your museum is "Buzz". The more buzz you have in your museum the more people come and donate/spend. Your buzz is based on the exhibits you have in your museum (along with how well you layout your museum, tours, decorations, etc.). In order to get great exhibits you need to send your staff on Expeditions. Based on the difficulty of the expeditions you get better fossils/fish/dinosaur bones etc. Therefore, staff management is very important in this game- leveling up your staff and training them is a crucial part of the game.  Also, your staff can die on expeditions- which really makes you invested in training them up properly.  When the staff return you get a loot crate which will have an exhibit piece inside, this feels like a loot box from other games- this adds some excitement to the game- Whats going to be inside??.  I love this mechanic!  So much fun.The game can get very detailed in your management of the museum, more than in past Two Point games. You can let it run by itself and do okay or you can micromanage prices and fees along with salaries and personnel to really optimize your museum.If you love Simulation games- I cannot recommend this game enough. Its been a long time since I played a game this good, let alone at release.

content: \n								I've been a huge fan of the Two Point series ever since Two Point Hospital successfully resurrected a genre classic. While I know Two Point Campus was a bit more mixed for many, I found I still liked the sauce even at the understandably more relaxed pace. But Two Point Museum is maybe their best game to date, which is a challenge when TPH had the chaos of trying to keep a hospital profitable, the patients alive, and the halls free of ghosts. Surely a museum can't possibly be that hard? Well...Okay well it's not THAT hard but that's actually a good thing. TPC's greatest weakness was long periods of idleness and TPH's weakness was obtuse objectives and the need for a perfect workflow that would get wrecked by shortcomings in the game's design. TPM dispenses with all of that - there's always something to focus on in the museum. I'm also impressed by how they've altered the game's level progression entirely - the last two games you just grabbed a hospital/school at random and went at it. This game actually comes up with more of a progression and eases you through it while also creating more of a feeling that there's a connected lore to it all. Also quite frankly they finally have a good use for decorations in this game that doesn't just require you to min-max in ignorance of the aesthetic design. Building museum exhibits is just plain fun and the gameplay system that requires you to decorate them is flexible enough to allow you to make them look cool without getting punished for not picking some OP item. I've had a blast building dinosaur rooms, ice caves, aquariums, and botanical gardens, and that's just what I've been able to touch. Gathering exhibits is actually something that takes careful planning but isn't overly painful - you have to send your staff out to do it and different skills help you avoid or gain certain event cards that aid or hinder your progress. And they have enough of a sense of humor to animate opening those mystery crates like a loot box. God bless em'.Oh and if you're a veteran... yes, your old pals on the radio station are back for another round of antics. You'd think three games in they might get rusty but actually the radio shows have somehow gotten funnier with each game. And of course our dear tannoy is back and she wants you to know she *despises children*. The humor and charm of this series has yet to wear on me. You'll probably start recognizing NPCs from the earlier games as well - several of the guest types are callbacks to students or patients from the last two games and given that I'm already hearing references to long term characters like Roderick Cushion and Tabitha Windsock, I'm expecting to see more of them as well. The Two Point team has successfully built a goofy universe across three games and I'm always here for more of it.I would say this is the first entry in the series that felt "cozy." TPH was all about constant chaos and mayhem, this game is about just making a cool museum that may or may not kill the guests but this time you're not responsible, the hospital down the road is! The challenges are far more manageable and the pace is more under my control than the game's. At one point I blew off an objective because I wanted to really put the design tools to the test and decorate my gardens and nothing broke! And now I like to think I have a *lovely* garden. I gather most people who played the old Bullfrog games are at a stage in their lives now (like me) where yea, that might be preferable! Just a good solid management game that isn't frustrating me because of some oblique mechanic that isn't working right.Frankly, I've loved every game in this series, and this one is fast becoming my favorite. But I like that all three of them have their own flavor and it feels easy to slip into one of the other entries when I'm interested in a different gameplay framework. This dev is 3 for 3 in my book and I'm so honestly happy to have been here since before TPH came out and the idea of a franchise was just a hopeful dream. Whatever the hell they tell me to build and manage next, I'm here. I can trust these guys to make games I *love*.I would also like to add that for once, I took the plunge on paying extra for early access and did NOT feel like I got ripped off for the privilege? Like I didn't feel like I spent an extra 10 quid for being a beta tester? The game is *finished*. I've had one crash, it may have just been Windows 11 anyway, and it happened when I tried making my assistants all dress up like Shadow the Hedhehog so really, that may have entirely been me.

content: \n								I've been a huge fan of the Two Point series ever since Two Point Hospital successfully resurrected a genre classic. While I know Two Point Campus was a bit more mixed for many, I found I still liked the sauce even at the understandably more relaxed pace. But Two Point Museum is maybe their best game to date, which is a challenge when TPH had the chaos of trying to keep a hospital profitable, the patients alive, and the halls free of ghosts. Surely a museum can't possibly be that hard? Well...Okay well it's not THAT hard but that's actually a good thing. TPC's greatest weakness was long periods of idleness and TPH's weakness was obtuse objectives and the need for a perfect workflow that would get wrecked by shortcomings in the game's design. TPM dispenses with all of that - there's always something to focus on in the museum. I'm also impressed by how they've altered the game's level progression entirely - the last two games you just grabbed a hospital/school at random and went at it. This game actually comes up with more of a progression and eases you through it while also creating more of a feeling that there's a connected lore to it all. Also quite frankly they finally have a good use for decorations in this game that doesn't just require you to min-max in ignorance of the aesthetic design. Building museum exhibits is just plain fun and the gameplay system that requires you to decorate them is flexible enough to allow you to make them look cool without getting punished for not picking some OP item. I've had a blast building dinosaur rooms, ice caves, aquariums, and botanical gardens, and that's just what I've been able to touch. Gathering exhibits is actually something that takes careful planning but isn't overly painful - you have to send your staff out to do it and different skills help you avoid or gain certain event cards that aid or hinder your progress. And they have enough of a sense of humor to animate opening those mystery crates like a loot box. God bless em'.Oh and if you're a veteran... yes, your old pals on the radio station are back for another round of antics. You'd think three games in they might get rusty but actually the radio shows have somehow gotten funnier with each game. And of course our dear tannoy is back and she wants you to know she *despises children*. The humor and charm of this series has yet to wear on me. You'll probably start recognizing NPCs from the earlier games as well - several of the guest types are callbacks to students or patients from the last two games and given that I'm already hearing references to long term characters like Roderick Cushion and Tabitha Windsock, I'm expecting to see more of them as well. The Two Point team has successfully built a goofy universe across three games and I'm always here for more of it.I would say this is the first entry in the series that felt "cozy." TPH was all about constant chaos and mayhem, this game is about just making a cool museum that may or may not kill the guests but this time you're not responsible, the hospital down the road is! The challenges are far more manageable and the pace is more under my control than the game's. At one point I blew off an objective because I wanted to really put the design tools to the test and decorate my gardens and nothing broke! And now I like to think I have a *lovely* garden. I gather most people who played the old Bullfrog games are at a stage in their lives now (like me) where yea, that might be preferable! Just a good solid management game that isn't frustrating me because of some oblique mechanic that isn't working right.Frankly, I've loved every game in this series, and this one is fast becoming my favorite. But I like that all three of them have their own flavor and it feels easy to slip into one of the other entries when I'm interested in a different gameplay framework. This dev is 3 for 3 in my book and I'm so honestly happy to have been here since before TPH came out and the idea of a franchise was just a hopeful dream. Whatever the hell they tell me to build and manage next, I'm here. I can trust these guys to make games I *love*.I would also like to add that for once, I took the plunge on paying extra for early access and did NOT feel like I got ripped off for the privilege? Like I didn't feel like I spent an extra 10 quid for being a beta tester? The game is *finished*. I've had one crash, it may have just been Windows 11 anyway, and it happened when I tried making my assistants all dress up like Shadow the Hedhehog so really, that may have entirely been me.
