content: \n								I've been a huge fan of the Two Point series ever since Two Point Hospital successfully resurrected a genre classic. While I know Two Point Campus was a bit more mixed for many, I found I still liked the sauce even at the understandably more relaxed pace. But Two Point Museum is maybe their best game to date, which is a challenge when TPH had the chaos of trying to keep a hospital profitable, the patients alive, and the halls free of ghosts. Surely a museum can't possibly be that hard? Well...Okay well it's not THAT hard but that's actually a good thing. TPC's greatest weakness was long periods of idleness and TPH's weakness was obtuse objectives and the need for a perfect workflow that would get wrecked by shortcomings in the game's design. TPM dispenses with all of that - there's always something to focus on in the museum. I'm also impressed by how they've altered the game's level progression entirely - the last two games you just grabbed a hospital/school at random and went at it. This game actually comes up with more of a progression and eases you through it while also creating more of a feeling that there's a connected lore to it all. Also quite frankly they finally have a good use for decorations in this game that doesn't just require you to min-max in ignorance of the aesthetic design. Building museum exhibits is just plain fun and the gameplay system that requires you to decorate them is flexible enough to allow you to make them look cool without getting punished for not picking some OP item. I've had a blast building dinosaur rooms, ice caves, aquariums, and botanical gardens, and that's just what I've been able to touch. Gathering exhibits is actually something that takes careful planning but isn't overly painful - you have to send your staff out to do it and different skills help you avoid or gain certain event cards that aid or hinder your progress. And they have enough of a sense of humor to animate opening those mystery crates like a loot box. God bless em'.Oh and if you're a veteran... yes, your old pals on the radio station are back for another round of antics. You'd think three games in they might get rusty but actually the radio shows have somehow gotten funnier with each game. And of course our dear tannoy is back and she wants you to know she *despises children*. The humor and charm of this series has yet to wear on me. You'll probably start recognizing NPCs from the earlier games as well - several of the guest types are callbacks to students or patients from the last two games and given that I'm already hearing references to long term characters like Roderick Cushion and Tabitha Windsock, I'm expecting to see more of them as well. The Two Point team has successfully built a goofy universe across three games and I'm always here for more of it.I would say this is the first entry in the series that felt "cozy." TPH was all about constant chaos and mayhem, this game is about just making a cool museum that may or may not kill the guests but this time you're not responsible, the hospital down the road is! The challenges are far more manageable and the pace is more under my control than the game's. At one point I blew off an objective because I wanted to really put the design tools to the test and decorate my gardens and nothing broke! And now I like to think I have a *lovely* garden. I gather most people who played the old Bullfrog games are at a stage in their lives now (like me) where yea, that might be preferable! Just a good solid management game that isn't frustrating me because of some oblique mechanic that isn't working right.Frankly, I've loved every game in this series, and this one is fast becoming my favorite. But I like that all three of them have their own flavor and it feels easy to slip into one of the other entries when I'm interested in a different gameplay framework. This dev is 3 for 3 in my book and I'm so honestly happy to have been here since before TPH came out and the idea of a franchise was just a hopeful dream. Whatever the hell they tell me to build and manage next, I'm here. I can trust these guys to make games I *love*.I would also like to add that for once, I took the plunge on paying extra for early access and did NOT feel like I got ripped off for the privilege? Like I didn't feel like I spent an extra 10 quid for being a beta tester? The game is *finished*. I've had one crash, it may have just been Windows 11 anyway, and it happened when I tried making my assistants all dress up like Shadow the Hedhehog so really, that may have entirely been me.

content: \n								I own, but never played Two Point Hospital and found the game play loop of Two Point Campus a bit shallow. Regardless, I found it charming and really like these types of games, so this was still worth an early purchase. Overall, I'd say this is a massive improvement over Hospital. I really enjoy that you now have to send out expeditions to find the items for your museum, with additional cosmetics unlocking at becoming available as you progress through the story. Since the staff members have real value due to these expeditions, it serves a key game play purpose to keep them happy and alive. It's an actual loss when your level 6 prehistory nerd falls down a crevice, never to be seen again. I also find that the guest and employees are not nearly as annoying with their wants and demands compared to the crybabies I had the unfortunate pleasure of selling overpriced degrees to in the previous game. Of the negatives, I find the zoning a bit cumbersome and not intuitive, especially with jobs like research and workstation, where it's not a continuous job. It would be nice to have some zones overlap, or be able to assign someone to more than one zone. I have some staff assigned to no zone, but they seem to laze about more than anything. I feel like once you get a pretty large staff, it is a lot of menus to see who is assigned to what and what jobs you have them selected for if you have some people solely focused of repairing vending machines and stuff and others cleaning, upgrading, etc. I also like how there is an actual campaign in this one, that encourages you to jump back and forth between multiple museums. It helps keep things fresh and not just abandoning one, to move onto another, as soon as you reach some arbitrary start level. I think the following is due to something wrong with my settings with my display or inside Nvidia Control Panel, but I started experiencing really bad frame rate issues when my museum got about half filled. Turning off VSync, which I think was enabled by default, seems to have resolved that though. Overall, I'm really impressed and excited to continue playing. I'm also excited to see what future themes they release. I feel like this is the perfect base for all kinds of awesome additional content later down the road.

content: \n ⇓ german below for my german friends ˙ᵕ˙ ⇓  Yes, yes, and one more time: YES!! I’m a huge fan of the Two Point series, and to be honest, I was a little worried at first about whether the new game would live up to expectations. Especially with so many games coming out lately that are, at best, just mediocre. Plus, I wasn’t sure how the whole museum concept would translate into exciting gameplay. But now? I couldn’t be happier—Two Point Museum is just insanely fun!After almost 13 hours of playtime, I can already say: this is my favorite game in the series. It’s fascinating how it still feels similar to Hospital and Campus at its core, yet delivers a completely fresh experience. Once again, you can easily sink hundreds of hours into it. And even if Hospital or Campus didn’t completely win you over, Museum might just be your thing. It plays noticeably different, while still keeping that signature Two Point charm.What really stands out to me about this one: it feels way more relaxing. In Two Point Hospital, I was constantly under pressure, like I had to keep up with a never-ending workload. But Museum has a much calmer vibe. There’s no rush—you can play at your own pace, which I find super enjoyable.On top of that, there’s just so much to discover, from exciting little details to hilarious moments. The attention to detail is incredible as always, and the expeditions are still fun even after the fiftieth time. Especially when my expert suddenly went “missing” and never came back—well, let’s just hope he’s thriving in the jungle!I’m beyond happy with my decision to grab the early-access version! Every hour of playtime has been an absolute blast, and technically, everything runs perfectly—zero crashes, zero bugs so far. I can’t recommend it enough. And if you don’t play it, you’re seriously missing out… especially since our beloved announcer voice is back with those legendary one-liners. ;)-------------------------------------------------------------------------- Ja, ja und nochmal: JA!! Ich bin ein riesiger Fan der Two-Point-Reihe und hatte ehrlich gesagt anfangs etwas Bedenken, ob der neue Teil mithalten kann. Gerade weil in letzter Zeit so viele Spiele erscheinen, die bestenfalls mittelmäßig sind und ich mir unsicher darüber war, wie sich das Konzept eines Museums in ein spannendes Gameplay verwandeln lässt. Umso glücklicher bin ich, dass Two Point Museum einfach nur unglaublich viel Spaß macht!Nach knapp 13 Stunden kann ich bereits sagen: Das ist mein liebster Teil der Reihe. Es ist faszinierend, wie das Spiel sich vom Grundprinzip her ähnlich wie Hospital und Campus anfühlt, aber trotzdem ein völlig neues Erlebnis bietet. Wieder einmal kann man hunderte Stunden darin versinken. Falls euch Hospital oder Campus nicht komplett überzeugt haben, könnte Museum trotzdem genau euer Ding sein. Es spielt sich nämlich spürbar anders, auch wenn es natürlich dem typischen Two-Point-Charme treu bleibt.Was für mich vor allem anders an diesem Teil ist: Das Spiel fühlt sich entspannter an. Während ich in Two Point Hospital oft unter gefühltem Dauerstrom stand, strahlt Museum eine angenehme Ruhe aus. Man wird nicht gehetzt und kann in seinem eigenen Tempo spielen, was ich als sehr angenehm empfinde.Zudem gibt es unfassbar viel zu entdecken, sowohl Spannendes als auch Lustiges. Die Liebe zum Detail ist wieder überall zu spüren, und die Expeditionen machen selbst nach der fünfzigsten Runde noch Laune. Besonders als mein Experte plötzlich „verschollen“ war und nicht zurückkam – na ja, hoffen wir mal, dass er sich im Dschungel gut eingelebt hat.Ich bin absolut happy mit meiner Entscheidung, die Vorab-Version gekauft zu haben! content: \n ⇓ german below for my german friends ˙ᵕ˙ ⇓  Yes, yes, and one more time: YES!! I’m a huge fan of the Two Point series, and to be honest, I was a little worried at first about whether the new game would live up to expectations. Especially with so many games coming out lately that are, at best, just mediocre. Plus, I wasn’t sure how the whole museum concept would translate into exciting gameplay. But now? I couldn’t be happier—Two Point Museum is just insanely fun!After almost 13 hours of playtime, I can already say: this is my favorite game in the series. It’s fascinating how it still feels similar to Hospital and Campus at its core, yet delivers a completely fresh experience. Once again, you can easily sink hundreds of hours into it. And even if Hospital or Campus didn’t completely win you over, Museum might just be your thing. It plays noticeably different, while still keeping that signature Two Point charm.What really stands out to me about this one: it feels way more relaxing. In Two Point Hospital, I was constantly under pressure, like I had to keep up with a never-ending workload. But Museum has a much calmer vibe. There’s no rush—you can play at your own pace, which I find super enjoyable.On top of that, there’s just so much to discover, from exciting little details to hilarious moments. The attention to detail is incredible as always, and the expeditions are still fun even after the fiftieth time. Especially when my expert suddenly went “missing” and never came back—well, let’s just hope he’s thriving in the jungle!I’m beyond happy with my decision to grab the early-access version! Every hour of playtime has been an absolute blast, and technically, everything runs perfectly—zero crashes, zero bugs so far. I can’t recommend it enough. And if you don’t play it, you’re seriously missing out… especially since our beloved announcer voice is back with those legendary one-liners. ;)-------------------------------------------------------------------------- Ja, ja und nochmal: JA!! Ich bin ein riesiger Fan der Two-Point-Reihe und hatte ehrlich gesagt anfangs etwas Bedenken, ob der neue Teil mithalten kann. Gerade weil in letzter Zeit so viele Spiele erscheinen, die bestenfalls mittelmäßig sind und ich mir unsicher darüber war, wie sich das Konzept eines Museums in ein spannendes Gameplay verwandeln lässt. Umso glücklicher bin ich, dass Two Point Museum einfach nur unglaublich viel Spaß macht!Nach knapp 13 Stunden kann ich bereits sagen: Das ist mein liebster Teil der Reihe. Es ist faszinierend, wie das Spiel sich vom Grundprinzip her ähnlich wie Hospital und Campus anfühlt, aber trotzdem ein völlig neues Erlebnis bietet. Wieder einmal kann man hunderte Stunden darin versinken. Falls euch Hospital oder Campus nicht komplett überzeugt haben, könnte Museum trotzdem genau euer Ding sein. Es spielt sich nämlich spürbar anders, auch wenn es natürlich dem typischen Two-Point-Charme treu bleibt.Was für mich vor allem anders an diesem Teil ist: Das Spiel fühlt sich entspannter an. Während ich in Two Point Hospital oft unter gefühltem Dauerstrom stand, strahlt Museum eine angenehme Ruhe aus. Man wird nicht gehetzt und kann in seinem eigenen Tempo spielen, was ich als sehr angenehm empfinde.Zudem gibt es unfassbar viel zu entdecken, sowohl Spannendes als auch Lustiges. Die Liebe zum Detail ist wieder überall zu spüren, und die Expeditionen machen selbst nach der fünfzigsten Runde noch Laune. Besonders als mein Experte plötzlich „verschollen“ war und nicht zurückkam – na ja, hoffen wir mal, dass er sich im Dschungel gut eingelebt hat.Ich bin absolut happy mit meiner Entscheidung, die Vorab-Version gekauft zu haben! Jede Spielstunde ist ein Heidenspaß, und technisch läuft alles einwandfrei – kein einziger Absturz oder Bug bisher. Ich kann es nur wärmstens empfehlen. Und wer es nicht spielt, verpasst definitiv etwas … vor allem, weil unsere altbekannte Durchsagen-Stimme wieder mit genialen Sprüchen am Start ist. ;)

I’m a huge fan of the Two Point series, and to be honest, I was a little worried at first about whether the new game would live up to expectations. Especially with so many games coming out lately that are, at best, just mediocre. Plus, I wasn’t sure how the whole museum concept would translate into exciting gameplay. But now? I couldn’t be happier—Two Point Museum is just insanely fun!After almost 13 hours of playtime, I can already say: this is my favorite game in the series. It’s fascinating how it still feels similar to Hospital and Campus at its core, yet delivers a completely fresh experience. Once again, you can easily sink hundreds of hours into it. And even if Hospital or Campus didn’t completely win you over, Museum might just be your thing. It plays noticeably different, while still keeping that signature Two Point charm.What really stands out to me about this one: it feels way more relaxing. In Two Point Hospital, I was constantly under pressure, like I had to keep up with a never-ending workload. But Museum has a much calmer vibe. There’s no rush—you can play at your own pace, which I find super enjoyable.On top of that, there’s just so much to discover, from exciting little details to hilarious moments. The attention to detail is incredible as always, and the expeditions are still fun even after the fiftieth time. Especially when my expert suddenly went “missing” and never came back—well, let’s just hope he’s thriving in the jungle!I’m beyond happy with my decision to grab the early-access version! Every hour of playtime has been an absolute blast, and technically, everything runs perfectly—zero crashes, zero bugs so far. I can’t recommend it enough. Umso glücklicher bin ich, dass Two Point Museum einfach nur unglaublich viel Spaß macht!Nach knapp 13 Stunden kann ich bereits sagen: Das ist mein liebster Teil der Reihe. Wieder einmal kann man hunderte Stunden darin versinken. Falls euch Hospital oder Campus nicht komplett überzeugt haben, könnte Museum trotzdem genau euer Ding sein. It makes the whole experience feel so much more alive!The creativity is off the charts, with fresh themes in every museum so far, new mechanics, and a huge variety of items to experiment with. From curating exhibits to keeping guests happy (and kids off the displays!), Two Point Museum is an absolute joy. I can’t believe I finally get to play a game where I build and run a museum!11/10, Two Point Studios—seriously, well done!

content: \n								The best Two Point game so far, taking the best parts of the Sim formula and world they have developed for Hospital and Campus to create an evolving experience that will test your museum management skills while also tickling your funny bone with their traditional wit.The game forgoes the traditional mission structure of prior Two Point games, instead tasking you with juggling managing several bespoke museums at the same time, managing to get appropriate Star levels at each stage to unlock new tools and experts that you can then use to advance your other museums.  Each museum also unlocks an Exploration Map that asks you to leverage your staff and various experts to complete challenges, puzzle through specific combinations of skills and tools, and steal, liberate, or 'discover' the relics back to your museum.Unlike prior Two Point games, where each theme plays similarly, Two Point Museum manages to make each broad category of artifact unique.  Prehistory exhibits contain a number of Multi-part skeletons that you have to dive back into the exploration map to find each piece for.  Botanical exhibits are often living creatures that require constant maintenance to prevent them from withering away, and a surprising number of which apply status effects to your guests that turn them into clowns, or vampires, or the like, and have different traits depending on how well they are maintained.  Many Marine life exhibits are fish that require special environments, feeding schedules, and cohabitants, requiring you to find just the right mix of fish for your aquarium management fix.  Your supernatural museum has a number of exhibits that might not sit well with the guests, and in a great twist, you get to also play hotel manager for your 'Polterguests' and find them just the right room where they can spend their afterlife in peace.I would state that at the time of this review, the Thievery mechanics may be a little too punishing.  Some thieves are just vandals and do some damage to an exhibit, whereas others will steal the exhibit and if you are lucky will attempt to ransom it back to you.  If an exhibit is stolen, its gone, and you will have to re-obtain it.  These mechanics are introduced a surprisingly deep way into the game, when you may have 2-3 established museums already, requiring you to rebuild your museum for security after expecting a fairly open campus like in prior games.In summary:Pros - Fresh mechanics for a Two Point gameTwo Point wit is on displayGame evolves over time, so its not the same mission repeating on a different mapDeep mechanics tailored for each broad artifact typeCons -More Punishing than other Two Point GamesSlower than other Two Point GamesNeed to design museum for thievery mechanics is not signposted early enoughI highly recommend this game, particularly for Two Point veterans!

content: \n								Rewriting my review after finishing all achievements and unlocking just about everything. Still very positive on the game. I've also played every Two Point game for 100ish hours each, and I feel this is the best one.I love how they have condensed the campaign down to five museums that you keep going back to as you choose. It's not shorter, you just spend more time in each location, and it's a lot of fun to go back to your first museum hours later to see how you can fix it up. There is no longer the feeling that you need to abandon your hard work and do it all over again. Each museum mostly focuses on one of the 7 exhibit types, prehistoric, supernatural, marine, space, and science, with botany and general exhibits also showing up from time to time. To earn more stars you continue working on those five museums. You're free to put as much stuff from any theme into any museum you choose, as all the maps are large enough to potentially hold everything in the game once you unlock all the plots. Progress is not timed at all, you can work towards the overarching goals at your leisure.I also love the move away from the room-based system. There are still plenty of rooms, but it doesn't have the same feel of just pasting the same templates over and over. Exhibits need to be put out into the spaces between the rooms, and you really don't know what exhibits you will find and how big they will be. You can benefit a lot from constantly rearranging and rethinking your museum layout. It's not just plop it down and forget it.I love how they improved the decoration system as well. Decorating rooms is similar to past games where you just put stuff in the rooms, but for the exhibits themselves you can see the radius of each decoration you're putting down and how it's affecting the exhibits. There's no longer some general decoration goal that's satisfied by just plopping down hundreds of things and hoping it goes up. You see exactly how each decoration affects its environment.I think this game improves on AI pathing, as well, I had a lot fewer issues with people getting stuck. The game might tell you people are stuck, but they resolve it on their own much more reliably than past games.The only negatives I can think of are that the thieves can be very annoying, and staff earn experience a little on the slow side. I love the idea of needing good security, my only issue is that I never really felt I could trust my staff to handle thieves on their own. They are bad at chasing thieves down even with speed traits, and some thief types would continue to steal even once exposed. Every time I have the mole thieves show up, a camera guy will spot them immediately, but if I don't manually plop a security guy on their heads, they might still get away with something because staff are just too slow to respond. Just wish the museum could be put into high alert mode for invasions or something like that. As far as staff exp goes, getting a max trained staff was the final achievement for me. It was a gift shop assistant reaching level 20 from 35 years working the gift shop nonstop. My experts going on hundreds of expeditions only reached level 10-12. Expeditions give far too little experience. This could also be infuriating if you manage to lose a staff member for some reason, as it's hard to train someone back in a reasonable amount of time.In any case, these issues are very minor to me in the grand scheme of the game. Thieves can be turned off entirely in sandbox mode. Speaking of sandbox, this mode is great for kids to learn the game, as you can virtually make the museum free to operate. My 5 year old is able to enjoy the game with zero experience in the genre or even with using a computer. Let's not forget the sound and music: they knocked it out of the park. I found myself humming the tunes from this game every day that I played it. Eventually some of the vocal announcements can become annoying, but you can just turn them off if you'd like.A final note: I play on a M1 Max Mac, and my sons play on the original M1, and the performance is really great. 450 people moving around your museum at once, and the game usually runs just fine. The only time I had it crash ever was when I alt-tabbed out and tried to come back a while later, but even that bug seems to have been fixed in recent patches. The game in general has gotten smoother with patches. I'm very pleased with its performance on a Mac.

content: \n								As someone who spent their childhood getting excited about museums... this is genuinely like a dream come true!Two Point Studios have really outdone themselves this time, and it shows. Not only is it very much in my wheelhouse thematically, but the game feels like it finally has just the right amount of creative freedom, having moved on from Campus and Hospital, and built on their foundations in a great and meaningful way. Gameplay and design choices feel more rewarding than ever, and I think I'll be playing this game a lot more than I did others in the series as a result. We really are getting to the point where the in-house formula of both management and creativity for the player, with that oh-so-great dash of humour, are, if not already- almost perfect. I think the devs must've enjoyed building this game and doing the R&D just as much as I've enjoyed playing it. My highlights include:+You can see just how much LOVE has been put into this game by the devs from Day 1+Absolutely beautiful graphics, lighting VFX, and colours, throughout- best yet in the series by far!+An iconic art style that continues to impress and advance 7 years after TPH started it all+Player creativity and design finally feels just as important as the management aspect, even in the tutorial+UI is well designed and user-friendly (Huge step up since Hospital particularly!)+The variety of new ideas and the themes have something to offer for everyone+There is SO much more variety this time around, each museum feels truly unique+The re-playability and gameplay loop is the best we've had so far, without feeling repetitive +The narration/announcements are hilariously on point; especially for anyone who has worked or spent a lot of time in museums/galleries/aquariums etc! =DI can't wait to see how players interact with this game, and I really do think that when we look back in years to come Two Point Museum will be a benchmark for future games not just in this series, but in the genre too.

Gameplay and design choices feel more rewarding than ever, and I think I'll be playing this game a lot more than I did others in the series as a result. We really are getting to the point where the in-house formula of both management and creativity for the player, with that oh-so-great dash of humour, are, if not already- almost perfect. I think the devs must've enjoyed building this game and doing the R&D just as much as I've enjoyed playing it. My highlights include:+You can see just how much LOVE has been put into this game by the devs from Day 1+Absolutely beautiful graphics, lighting VFX, and colours, throughout- best yet in the series by far!+An iconic art style that continues to impress and advance 7 years after TPH started it all+Player creativity and design finally feels just as important as the management aspect, even in the tutorial+UI is well designed and user-friendly (Huge step up since Hospital particularly!)+The variety of new ideas and the themes have something to offer for everyone+There is SO much more variety this time around, each museum feels truly unique+The re-playability and gameplay loop is the best we've had so far, without feeling repetitive +The narration/announcements are hilariously on point; especially for anyone who has worked or spent a lot of time in museums/galleries/aquariums etc! =DI can't wait to see how players interact with this game, and I really do think that when we look back in years to come Two Point Museum will be a benchmark for future games not just in this series, but in the genre too.

content: \n								I am a big fan of Two Point Hospital and was looking forward to this game, enough to buy the version whereas I could have early access. I am enjoying the museum iteration of the franchise thus far! You have similar concepts in constructing rooms with functions, employees with character traits, but you have a bit of difference in that there's the overall picture of making your museum pleasing on a wide variety of factors which makes the game feel more tycoon feeling in essence than perhaps the hospital version was. If you've not played any of the Two Point games before, I think you'll still enjoy this game. The way this series introduces you to concepts of the gameplay is very 'newb' friendly and explains things so you are not left wondering how to do anything. You still have to figure out how to best do things to succeed, like who to hire, how to place exhibits or decor, etc... but all the basics are laid out for you easy peasy.I am happy I got the version that allowed early access and an additional 5k kudos. Noticeably, there are items that are cheap kudos prices (5-25kudos), which is extremely nice when I compare it to TP Hospital, where it seemed like everything worth getting is 200-500 kudos. I've been able to get a bunch of nice little extras thus far. I could do without the added Sonic items, as I'm not a huge Sonic fan and I think they never really fit appropriately in any type of setting. I get it though, the publisher is SEGA. But kinda wish they would offer something a bit more...generally desirable.I have to say though, my high end gaming laptop wants to struggle slightly with the game, though it far exceeds the recommended specs. So be warned, it seems like it has high system requirements, moreso than they let on. I always play games on 'Ultra' graphics and highest settings, but find I am going to have to lower my settings in order to reduce some lag I do experience, which unfortunately is noticeable.Overall, I do recommend this game. The concept makes it fun, they throw in a smidge of humor, and the graphics are nice.

content: \n								I think they have finally found the perfect balance.Two point hospital was always a bit too hectic and I always felt I was reacting because I didn't know what diseases would come next or what I would need (except in scenarios second time around)Two point campus gave you all the control and you could really plan ahead but it was... a bit stale... you set up, and then you watch the year go by with barely any input... Train he teachers to the desired level, and once you have all the rooms.. you are done.Museum has struck an amazing balance, you have control  and are in charge of the speed of the game through the expeditions, but there are no long stretches of nothing, because you can always be getting new exhibits and tweaking the museum if you want. Or if you want to redecorate a whole wing don't send any expeditions for a bit and slow down the game to let you deal with that... or buy a second helicopter and have more staff, and salaries, go on expeditions, with new exhibits to delight your guests or analyse for knowledge.There are a ton of exhibits to collect and even when you get a repeat one (I got a bunch of plebians trying co complete the cursed animatronics) you can get knowledge (which makes your actual exhibit better) and even after you reach top knowledge on an exhibit, analysing it gives you money and helps unlock themed items to make your museum better.Staff is better as well, with a return to the 1 thing per slot of two point hospital, and they level up quite slowly so having them injuried or worse... MIA has a much larger impact vs the hire and fire of the past and the training room is a lot more compact, which is a plusAll the staff can and often need to go in expeditions, and skills can have suprise uses (customer service to get a positive effect on a ghost hunt or positive feelings to avoid a curse) as well as the skills that are explicitly about expeditions (survival, surveying, piloting) between that and the traits, the hunt for the perfect guy is ONJanitors have had the upgrade and repair skill merged which is good and do their usual stuff. Ticket booth is the new "library" specialist assistant, The experts are the backbone of mainting exhibits and going on expeditions. It's all good. It gets challenging when expeditions need many, varied staff and it puts a strain on your staffing levels at homeThe decoration system is also very engaging, with each exhibit becoming better if decorated and also often having specific goals to meet (EG have X decoration nearby or be near a Y theme exhibit). But it's not so hard that you can't plonk some stuff around if you don't have a great artistic eye and then figure things from thereIn conclusion: Balance and control. Or if you want to redecorate a whole wing don't send any expeditions for a bit and slow down the game to let you deal with that... or buy a second helicopter and have more staff, and salaries, go on expeditions, with new exhibits to delight your guests or analyse for knowledge.There are a ton of exhibits to collect and even when you get a repeat one (I got a bunch of plebians trying co complete the cursed animatronics) you can get knowledge (which makes your actual exhibit better) and even after you reach top knowledge on an exhibit, analysing it gives you money and helps unlock themed items to make your museum better.Staff is better as well, with a return to the 1 thing per slot of two point hospital, and they level up quite slowly so having them injuried or worse... MIA has a much larger impact vs the hire and fire of the past and the training room is a lot more compact, which is a plusAll the staff can and often need to go in expeditions, and skills can have suprise uses (customer service to get a positive effect on a ghost hunt or positive feelings to avoid a curse) as well as the skills that are explicitly about expeditions (survival, surveying, piloting) between that and the traits, the hunt for the perfect guy is ONJanitors have had the upgrade and repair skill merged which is good and do their usual stuff. Ticket booth is the new "library" specialist assistant, The experts are the backbone of mainting exhibits and going on expeditions. It's all good. It gets challenging when expeditions need many, varied staff and it puts a strain on your staffing levels at homeThe decoration system is also very engaging, with each exhibit becoming better if decorated and also often having specific goals to meet (EG have X decoration nearby or be near a Y theme exhibit). But it's not so hard that you can't plonk some stuff around if you don't have a great artistic eye and then figure things from thereIn conclusion: Balance and control. Expeditions are challenging but not punishing, and you can decide if you want to take it slow and safe or push for some risk and reward. Decoration system encourages you to decorate, but you don't need to obsess with it. But must importantly I never feel overwhelmed with things coming off left field like in Hospital, because I control what expeditions I want to go on and therefore what kind of exhibit  (but not the exact exhibit) I get, but there is no long stretches in nothing like in Campus, because you can always go on another expedition.

Fun new fresh ideas, animations and designs are better than ever, and probably more assets to design and play with than before.+ The simulation/management aspects are fleshed out and offer a surprising amount of depth. There is no shortage of new mechanics and they all are intuitive. No crazy learning curves but there's room to manage if you're into that.- Training is both tedious and mostly unnecessary, until it's not and then it's a pain to train.- Expeditions are just timer mechanics that are cumbersome and hard to navigate. The loot box mechanics are kinda fun, but also kinda bizarre for this game. The system just doesn't mesh with the rest of the game loop.- There are 5 main levels (and some mini levels I recommend skipping) and, unlike the last two point games, you play them all at once? I see why the devs settled on this direction but it leads to a sense of incompleteness to each level. Once I finish playing, I won't ever come back to this one because it would be like starting a game halfway through and trying to remember what I was doing. The level progression design is simply an obstacle to complete playthroughs, and management games aren't a genre that should be hard to jump back in at any point.

content: \n								I think it's safe to say that this is the best Two Point game yet in a series of already pretty great games. Museum feels more creative, more complex, and more full of charm and mechanical depth than either Hospital or University. My meager playtime so far has all been in a few absolutely engrossing sessions and I've found the game hard to put down.The pacing is a bit different than Hospital, which shipped you off to a new hospital after you got your full 3 stars on your current level. Here, there are fewer museums but each caps out at a certain point and encourages you to go to another museum and build that one up to learn some new mechanics before coming back to apply what you've learned. I wasn't sure if I'd like that change at first, but it keeps the pacing up (you're not stuck in one place for too long) and returning to your older museums with new toys is a lot of fun. There are some quibbles, the UI is largely excellent for a game like this but even so I find myself missing information. For instance, there's no overview to show litter. Another missing feature I'd like is an overview of all available jobs in the museum so I know when to hire more staff. Right now it's a bit of a guessing game by looking at the staff list and seeing who's busy etc. But overall, you can tell this is the third iteration of an idea because the UI contains a ton of information, is fun to look at, and mostly easy to navigate. There's a lot more to say but the top line is buy Two Point Museum if you're interested in management games at all, or want to give them a go. The Two Point games are easily the most accessible and chill, and Two Point Museum looks to be the best of them.

content: \n								I'll preface this by drawing attention to my playtime, 2.7h is not very long and my issues may well be resolved later on, but I'm very tempted to shelve the game at this point.My issue is the apparent gameplay loop, it's a lot of waiting and very little doing in my experience. See the way this works is that you manage a museum, museums need exhibits and it's your job to present these exhibits. In order to get the exhibits you send out expeditions and these take time to complete, not overly long but it's not instant.This causes a gameplay loop which consists of you setting up the support rooms like staff room, souvenir shop, toilets and such with your starting funds. Then you send out an expedition and wait for them to return with a random exhibit, which you set up. Then you do it again, send out an expedition, wait for it to complete, set up exhibit and send the next expedition.I'm missing something to do while the expedition is completing, from my experience there's nothing. Just wait for it to complete, set up the exhibit, send the next expedition and wait again.As I'm writing this I started to compare it to Planet Zoo and I came to realise that the fact that the exhibits are semi-random and not all available for me to plan around makes my museum feel less personal. I'm not really in control of what is exhibited in the museum, not in the same way as I were in Planet Zoo.In Planet Zoo I could plan ahead and make my bear-focused park and disregard the elephants because they are just oversized grey pigs with long snouts, whatever I wanted that's what I created. It meant that my zoo was mine.In Two Point Museum I'm handed specific exhibits one at a time when the expeditions return, I have the option of displaying it or not. But if I don't display it, then I'm just back to waiting around for the next one, with no progress made. But my experience with the game (less than 3h) have been pretty disappointing. There's no doubt that the presentation is excellent and the humour is great, but the gameplay is less than stellar with way to much waiting around and to little control.

In order to get the exhibits you send out expeditions and these take time to complete, not overly long but it's not instant.This causes a gameplay loop which consists of you setting up the support rooms like staff room, souvenir shop, toilets and such with your starting funds. Then you send out an expedition and wait for them to return with a random exhibit, which you set up. Then you do it again, send out an expedition, wait for it to complete, set up exhibit and send the next expedition.I'm missing something to do while the expedition is completing, from my experience there's nothing. Just wait for it to complete, set up the exhibit, send the next expedition and wait again.As I'm writing this I started to compare it to Planet Zoo and I came to realise that the fact that the exhibits are semi-random and not all available for me to plan around makes my museum feel less personal. I'm not really in control of what is exhibited in the museum, not in the same way as I were in Planet Zoo.In Planet Zoo I could plan ahead and make my bear-focused park and disregard the elephants because they are just oversized grey pigs with long snouts, whatever I wanted that's what I created. It meant that my zoo was mine.In Two Point Museum I'm handed specific exhibits one at a time when the expeditions return, I have the option of displaying it or not. But if I don't display it, then I'm just back to waiting around for the next one, with no progress made. It makes the museum feel less personal since I'm not in control of what's displayed, only *how* it's displayed.Maybe my expectations were off or maybe the issues resolve themselves later in the campaign or in the sandbox. But my experience with the game (less than 3h) have been pretty disappointing. There's no doubt that the presentation is excellent and the humour is great, but the gameplay is less than stellar with way to much waiting around and to little control.

content: \n								I'm a big strategy fan, and I've played hundreds of simulators, management, and builder games. Strategy is a my favorite genre. And at first glance, I thought I wouldn't play TPM. But after seeing the overwhelmingly positive reviews, which is rather rare for strategy games, I thought I'd give it a try.I'm only 3 hours in after playing campaign and sandbox, and I'm already bored.Why?TPM is slow and repetitive. It doesn't take long before you realize that every time you play, you'll find the same items and follow a nearly identical progression path every time you play the game. Randomness and openness of the game doesn't really seem there. This is a very linear type strategy game.So most of the "learning" curve of the game comes from directing the flow of patrons through your museum and placing security cams and having appropriate staff to avoid thieves and collect money. The actual placement of objects in rooms and building the room is mostly trivial and the expeditions are nothing more than busy work. To make the busy work even more busy-worky, you will can dissect your duplicate busy work expedition finds to gain "knowledge". And decorating is basically just spamming information boards and random decorations that match the theme of the item you're decorating around.The announcer is funny at first, but quickly starts to sound like a Karen cracking lame nonstop jokes. And all the characters acting like they are Mr. Bean is cute at first but then gets kind of yawn inducing. Which I guess is this games style so it's forgivable. Just a little too silly for my taste. Also, why do I have to watch a crate box bounce up and down before shooting out my expedition finds every single time, like I am opening card packs from a p2w mobile game? eww stop What would have made TPM fun for me would have been some sense of randomness or random generation. When I send out an expedition, I want to have know idea what I'm going to find. I want every playthrough to be unique and every museum to start out differentely due to randomness. I don't want to randomly earn a torch decoration or decal decoration for doing nothing, and there is absolutely no reason I should have to place info boards manually when they are basically necessary for all the exibits. Perhaps the museum could be approached by art dealers and you could visit collectors to find items you don't just find via expedition. content: \n								I'm a big strategy fan, and I've played hundreds of simulators, management, and builder games. Strategy is a my favorite genre. And at first glance, I thought I wouldn't play TPM. But after seeing the overwhelmingly positive reviews, which is rather rare for strategy games, I thought I'd give it a try.I'm only 3 hours in after playing campaign and sandbox, and I'm already bored.Why?TPM is slow and repetitive. It doesn't take long before you realize that every time you play, you'll find the same items and follow a nearly identical progression path every time you play the game. Randomness and openness of the game doesn't really seem there. This is a very linear type strategy game.So most of the "learning" curve of the game comes from directing the flow of patrons through your museum and placing security cams and having appropriate staff to avoid thieves and collect money. The actual placement of objects in rooms and building the room is mostly trivial and the expeditions are nothing more than busy work. To make the busy work even more busy-worky, you will can dissect your duplicate busy work expedition finds to gain "knowledge". And decorating is basically just spamming information boards and random decorations that match the theme of the item you're decorating around.The announcer is funny at first, but quickly starts to sound like a Karen cracking lame nonstop jokes. And all the characters acting like they are Mr. Bean is cute at first but then gets kind of yawn inducing. Which I guess is this games style so it's forgivable. Just a little too silly for my taste. Also, why do I have to watch a crate box bounce up and down before shooting out my expedition finds every single time, like I am opening card packs from a p2w mobile game? eww stop What would have made TPM fun for me would have been some sense of randomness or random generation. When I send out an expedition, I want to have know idea what I'm going to find. I want every playthrough to be unique and every museum to start out differentely due to randomness. I don't want to randomly earn a torch decoration or decal decoration for doing nothing, and there is absolutely no reason I should have to place info boards manually when they are basically necessary for all the exibits. Perhaps the museum could be approached by art dealers and you could visit collectors to find items you don't just find via expedition. Give us options from the jump so that we have some sense of choice. So here I am 3 hours in debating another go so that I can squeeze a little more out of the museum, but I am dreading going through the same progression where I know I'll be placing a starfish fossil, a casette tape fossile, and the same couple dinosaur skeletons you find everytime you start. And then hiring the Mr. Bean goons who are going to do the same stupid stuff like walk in tar pits and then randomly walk around the museum with tar feet. Yawn. Too simple, silly, and unchallenging, and most clicks are more busy work that actual management. And even fast mode is too slow. From what I read, people are getting dumber and 25% of the adult population is illiterate. I imagine it's similar for the rest of the world as well. So maybe this is where we are now? That's the only way this game is getting an overwhelmingly positive review score. Because anyone who wants a real sense of exploration and randomness or desires a more thought and strategy would not rate this positively. But perhaps people can't see that this game is mostly just busy work clicking and you'll mostly spend hours repeating the same motion and every playthough will be very similar.Again, I am just 3 hours in so maybe there is a lot more depth after 10, 20, 30 hours. I dunno. But should I havey to do hours of what feels like busy work to get captured by a strategy game. The first few hours should be the most exciting and I should want to play it over and over again.If this is your first strategy game or you're in middle school or low IQ, this might be a nice introduction to simple strategy and management. But I can't recommend this to anyone who wants to feel that deep strategy vibe

content: \n								I'm a big strategy fan, and I've played hundreds of simulators, management, and builder games. Strategy is a my favorite genre. And at first glance, I thought I wouldn't play TPM. But after seeing the overwhelmingly positive reviews, which is rather rare for strategy games, I thought I'd give it a try.I'm only 3 hours in after playing campaign and sandbox, and I'm already bored.Why?TPM is slow and repetitive. It doesn't take long before you realize that every time you play, you'll find the same items and follow a nearly identical progression path every time you play the game. Randomness and openness of the game doesn't really seem there. This is a very linear type strategy game.So most of the "learning" curve of the game comes from directing the flow of patrons through your museum and placing security cams and having appropriate staff to avoid thieves and collect money. The actual placement of objects in rooms and building the room is mostly trivial and the expeditions are nothing more than busy work. To make the busy work even more busy-worky, you will can dissect your duplicate busy work expedition finds to gain "knowledge". And decorating is basically just spamming information boards and random decorations that match the theme of the item you're decorating around.The announcer is funny at first, but quickly starts to sound like a Karen cracking lame nonstop jokes. And all the characters acting like they are Mr. Bean is cute at first but then gets kind of yawn inducing. Which I guess is this games style so it's forgivable. Just a little too silly for my taste. Also, why do I have to watch a crate box bounce up and down before shooting out my expedition finds every single time, like I am opening card packs from a p2w mobile game? eww stop What would have made TPM fun for me would have been some sense of randomness or random generation. When I send out an expedition, I want to have know idea what I'm going to find. I want every playthrough to be unique and every museum to start out differentely due to randomness. I don't want to randomly earn a torch decoration or decal decoration for doing nothing, and there is absolutely no reason I should have to place info boards manually when they are basically necessary for all the exibits. Perhaps the museum could be approached by art dealers and you could visit collectors to find items you don't just find via expedition. Give us options from the jump so that we have some sense of choice. So here I am 3 hours in debating another go so that I can squeeze a little more out of the museum, but I am dreading going through the same progression where I know I'll be placing a starfish fossil, a casette tape fossile, and the same couple dinosaur skeletons you find everytime you start. And then hiring the Mr. Bean goons who are going to do the same stupid stuff like walk in tar pits and then randomly walk around the museum with tar feet. Yawn. Too simple, silly, and unchallenging, and most clicks are more busy work that actual management. And even fast mode is too slow. From what I read, people are getting dumber and 25% of the adult population is illiterate. I imagine it's similar for the rest of the world as well. So maybe this is where we are now? That's the only way this game is getting an overwhelmingly positive review score. Because anyone who wants a real sense of exploration and randomness or desires a more thought and strategy would not rate this positively. But perhaps people can't see that this game is mostly just busy work clicking and you'll mostly spend hours repeating the same motion and every playthough will be very similar.Again, I am just 3 hours in so maybe there is a lot more depth after 10, 20, 30 hours. I dunno. But should I havey to do hours of what feels like busy work to get captured by a strategy game. The first few hours should be the most exciting and I should want to play it over and over again.If this is your first strategy game or you're in middle school or low IQ, this might be a nice introduction to simple strategy and management. But I can't recommend this to anyone who wants to feel that deep strategy vibe

content: \n								I'm a big strategy fan, and I've played hundreds of simulators, management, and builder games. Strategy is a my favorite genre. And at first glance, I thought I wouldn't play TPM. But after seeing the overwhelmingly positive reviews, which is rather rare for strategy games, I thought I'd give it a try.I'm only 3 hours in after playing campaign and sandbox, and I'm already bored.Why?TPM is slow and repetitive. It doesn't take long before you realize that every time you play, you'll find the same items and follow a nearly identical progression path every time you play the game. Randomness and openness of the game doesn't really seem there. This is a very linear type strategy game.So most of the "learning" curve of the game comes from directing the flow of patrons through your museum and placing security cams and having appropriate staff to avoid thieves and collect money. The actual placement of objects in rooms and building the room is mostly trivial and the expeditions are nothing more than busy work. To make the busy work even more busy-worky, you will can dissect your duplicate busy work expedition finds to gain "knowledge". And decorating is basically just spamming information boards and random decorations that match the theme of the item you're decorating around.The announcer is funny at first, but quickly starts to sound like a Karen cracking lame nonstop jokes. And all the characters acting like they are Mr. Bean is cute at first but then gets kind of yawn inducing. Which I guess is this games style so it's forgivable. Just a little too silly for my taste. Also, why do I have to watch a crate box bounce up and down before shooting out my expedition finds every single time, like I am opening card packs from a p2w mobile game? eww stop What would have made TPM fun for me would have been some sense of randomness or random generation. When I send out an expedition, I want to have know idea what I'm going to find. I want every playthrough to be unique and every museum to start out differentely due to randomness. I don't want to randomly earn a torch decoration or decal decoration for doing nothing, and there is absolutely no reason I should have to place info boards manually when they are basically necessary for all the exibits. Perhaps the museum could be approached by art dealers and you could visit collectors to find items you don't just find via expedition. Give us options from the jump so that we have some sense of choice. So here I am 3 hours in debating another go so that I can squeeze a little more out of the museum, but I am dreading going through the same progression where I know I'll be placing a starfish fossil, a casette tape fossile, and the same couple dinosaur skeletons you find everytime you start. And then hiring the Mr. Bean goons who are going to do the same stupid stuff like walk in tar pits and then randomly walk around the museum with tar feet. Yawn. Too simple, silly, and unchallenging, and most clicks are more busy work that actual management. And even fast mode is too slow. From what I read, people are getting dumber and 25% of the adult population is illiterate. I imagine it's similar for the rest of the world as well. So maybe this is where we are now? That's the only way this game is getting an overwhelmingly positive review score. Because anyone who wants a real sense of exploration and randomness or desires a more thought and strategy would not rate this positively. But perhaps people can't see that this game is mostly just busy work clicking and you'll mostly spend hours repeating the same motion and every playthough will be very similar.Again, I am just 3 hours in so maybe there is a lot more depth after 10, 20, 30 hours. I dunno. But should I havey to do hours of what feels like busy work to get captured by a strategy game. The first few hours should be the most exciting and I should want to play it over and over again.If this is your first strategy game or you're in middle school or low IQ, this might be a nice introduction to simple strategy and management. But I can't recommend this to anyone who wants to feel that deep strategy vibe

content: \n								I'm a big strategy fan, and I've played hundreds of simulators, management, and builder games. Strategy is a my favorite genre. And at first glance, I thought I wouldn't play TPM. But after seeing the overwhelmingly positive reviews, which is rather rare for strategy games, I thought I'd give it a try.I'm only 3 hours in after playing campaign and sandbox, and I'm already bored.Why?TPM is slow and repetitive. It doesn't take long before you realize that every time you play, you'll find the same items and follow a nearly identical progression path every time you play the game. Randomness and openness of the game doesn't really seem there. This is a very linear type strategy game.So most of the "learning" curve of the game comes from directing the flow of patrons through your museum and placing security cams and having appropriate staff to avoid thieves and collect money. The actual placement of objects in rooms and building the room is mostly trivial and the expeditions are nothing more than busy work. To make the busy work even more busy-worky, you will can dissect your duplicate busy work expedition finds to gain "knowledge". And decorating is basically just spamming information boards and random decorations that match the theme of the item you're decorating around.The announcer is funny at first, but quickly starts to sound like a Karen cracking lame nonstop jokes. And all the characters acting like they are Mr. Bean is cute at first but then gets kind of yawn inducing. Which I guess is this games style so it's forgivable. Just a little too silly for my taste. Also, why do I have to watch a crate box bounce up and down before shooting out my expedition finds every single time, like I am opening card packs from a p2w mobile game? eww stop What would have made TPM fun for me would have been some sense of randomness or random generation. When I send out an expedition, I want to have know idea what I'm going to find. I want every playthrough to be unique and every museum to start out differentely due to randomness. I don't want to randomly earn a torch decoration or decal decoration for doing nothing, and there is absolutely no reason I should have to place info boards manually when they are basically necessary for all the exibits. Perhaps the museum could be approached by art dealers and you could visit collectors to find items you don't just find via expedition. Give us options from the jump so that we have some sense of choice. So here I am 3 hours in debating another go so that I can squeeze a little more out of the museum, but I am dreading going through the same progression where I know I'll be placing a starfish fossil, a casette tape fossile, and the same couple dinosaur skeletons you find everytime you start. And then hiring the Mr. Bean goons who are going to do the same stupid stuff like walk in tar pits and then randomly walk around the museum with tar feet. Yawn. Too simple, silly, and unchallenging, and most clicks are more busy work that actual management. And even fast mode is too slow. From what I read, people are getting dumber and 25% of the adult population is illiterate. I imagine it's similar for the rest of the world as well. So maybe this is where we are now? That's the only way this game is getting an overwhelmingly positive review score. Because anyone who wants a real sense of exploration and randomness or desires a more thought and strategy would not rate this positively. But perhaps people can't see that this game is mostly just busy work clicking and you'll mostly spend hours repeating the same motion and every playthough will be very similar.Again, I am just 3 hours in so maybe there is a lot more depth after 10, 20, 30 hours. I dunno. But should I havey to do hours of what feels like busy work to get captured by a strategy game. The first few hours should be the most exciting and I should want to play it over and over again.If this is your first strategy game or you're in middle school or low IQ, this might be a nice introduction to simple strategy and management. But I can't recommend this to anyone who wants to feel that deep strategy vibe

content: \n								I'm 58 hours in so far with all of my museums at 4 stars in campaign mode but I have to say this game has been terribly addictive.  It hits so many check boxes for me offering a game that has a wonderful strategic element, allows you some creativity and has a good sense of humour.I've only played Two-Point Hospital and I wish I had tried University. That said, I find Museum to be leaps and bounds better than Hospital. With Hospital, every new hospital was just an iteration of the last with a couple new illnesses to treat. WIth Museum, every new museum is an entirely new adventure with it's own distinct flavour and feel and with it's own distinct mechanics you need to worry about. You start with a vanilla prehistory museum and everything seems straightforward. You collect fossils and artefacts to display. You may also find plants which requires you to at times set up humidifiers and heaters.You then move off to either the Haunted Mansion or the Aquarium. With the Haunted Mansion you are now not only dealing with haunted artefacts to display but also ghosts each with their own needs that will need to be kept in guest rooms. If they get upset, they break out and terrorise your guests.The aquarium deals with fish and different fish, again, have different needs including water temperature and types of food. You can even breed fish.Then it's off to desert to mine metals and create inventions to display followed by a museum filled with space artefacts that can power and activate each other when they are in close proximity.It's all quite varied and interesting. There's still an underlying grind. You send out a team to a site to search for artefacts (or better quality versions of the same artefact), unlock new sites, then repeat as you complete quests for your museum.Everything seems to work as it should with no big hiccups and surprises. I still don't like the design of Two-Point's NPCs ( those eyes :-\ ) but watching them mill about is incredibly entertaining.If you liked any of the Two-Point games or enjoy strategy games, this is pretty much a must-own.

content: \n								Another amazing management game put out by Two Point Studios, the third in their series from Two Point Hospital, Two Point Campus, and now Two Point Museum. I'll first talk about my thoughts on this game and then how it compares to the previous two. The game has you managing museums which can be down via a career mode as well as Sandbox. The primary gameplay loop is placing exhibits to attract guest, improve those exhibits, collecting more types of exhibits, and finally the balance of keeping an income, tackling various challenges of management.There is a lot of depth to the mechanics in the game. An exhibit has multiple aspects from Buzz, knowledge, entertainment and traits it can have. One of the most interesting parts of the game are there are different types of exhibits that behave differently. For example your standard prehistoric exhibit an object you place and mostly make sure is clean.Now you can still upgrade that exbit and do things to increase it's knowledge and buzz. Yet, other types of exhibits such as an Aquarium for fish has different needs and setup. Different fish need different water temp, some fish can eat other fish. Haunted exhibits allow you to collection ghost for display which can escape and cause panic if certain things are not met. And you're free to mix and match, and basically required to do this for museum. It's not that you museum can only have one type you can certain specialize in being primary focused on one type but often will have multiple. There are other mechanics in place when it comes to sending out expeditions to find new museums or collect more of an artifacts to improve its knowledge bonus. You can setup tours and run marketing campaigns. Different types of guest have different wants, and so on. It leads to a very fun gameplay loop with enough depth to really play around with, but not so much you can't pick it up intuitively.Finally I think it is important to compare it to the previous two games in the Two Point series. Since they all have the same skeleton. To get it out of the way, I think Museum is plenty different from the other two where it doesn't feel like the previous games with a different skin. There are some core elements that cross over which isnt a bad thing, but many mechanics are added or change up enough it provides a much different experience. If you enjoyed either of the previous games this you will enjoy easily. If you werent a fan of either game this probably won't pull you in unless the idea of a Museum really appeals to you. If you liked Hospital but weren't a fan of Campus, I think this is a better game and most would enjoy it. Since a criticism for some with Campus was it was a bit too similar to hospital though I didn't agree with that. I also think this game show Two Point is continuing to improve on their formula for making management games. Maybe the best example of this is the improved customization. Specifically with more types/themes and more control on walls, floors, and fencing you can place. The last part I would like to touch on is difficulty. I found Two Point Hospital a great challenge when you got to later levels or DLC levels. Two Point Campus I found way to easy. I enjoyed Campus but the game was IMO incredibility easy. TPH I at times of fail missions or really struggle to get that 3rd Star in some levels. In TPC never once failed a level and 3 starred all base game levels with out literally have a single student fail out let alone ever get a grade lower than a B. This game provide challenge in a couple levels where you have to play at a decent level to not only hit challenge Stars but to keep a budget. TLDR: Fantastic game, a great improvement on the Two Point Series, and highly recommend.

I'll first talk about my thoughts on this game and then how it compares to the previous two. The game has you managing museums which can be down via a career mode as well as Sandbox. The primary gameplay loop is placing exhibits to attract guest, improve those exhibits, collecting more types of exhibits, and finally the balance of keeping an income, tackling various challenges of management.There is a lot of depth to the mechanics in the game. An exhibit has multiple aspects from Buzz, knowledge, entertainment and traits it can have. One of the most interesting parts of the game are there are different types of exhibits that behave differently. For example your standard prehistoric exhibit an object you place and mostly make sure is clean.Now you can still upgrade that exbit and do things to increase it's knowledge and buzz. Yet, other types of exhibits such as an Aquarium for fish has different needs and setup. Different fish need different water temp, some fish can eat other fish. Haunted exhibits allow you to collection ghost for display which can escape and cause panic if certain things are not met. And you're free to mix and match, and basically required to do this for museum. It's not that you museum can only have one type you can certain specialize in being primary focused on one type but often will have multiple. There are other mechanics in place when it comes to sending out expeditions to find new museums or collect more of an artifacts to improve its knowledge bonus. You can setup tours and run marketing campaigns. Different types of guest have different wants, and so on. It leads to a very fun gameplay loop with enough depth to really play around with, but not so much you can't pick it up intuitively.Finally I think it is important to compare it to the previous two games in the Two Point series. Since they all have the same skeleton. To get it out of the way, I think Museum is plenty different from the other two where it doesn't feel like the previous games with a different skin. There are some core elements that cross over which isnt a bad thing, but many mechanics are added or change up enough it provides a much different experience. If you enjoyed either of the previous games this you will enjoy easily. If you werent a fan of either game this probably won't pull you in unless the idea of a Museum really appeals to you. If you liked Hospital but weren't a fan of Campus, I think this is a better game and most would enjoy it. Since a criticism for some with Campus was it was a bit too similar to hospital though I didn't agree with that. I also think this game show Two Point is continuing to improve on their formula for making management games. Maybe the best example of this is the improved customization. In TPC never once failed a level and 3 starred all base game levels with out literally have a single student fail out let alone ever get a grade lower than a B. TLDR: Fantastic game, a great improvement on the Two Point Series, and highly recommend.

content: \n								Note: This is my first Two-Point game I have played.I highly recommend this cozy Museum simulator. There are so many cute and funny details that I still find every time I play. There are enough different themes so that things don't feel repetitive, and as you progress through the different locations, you aren't assaulted by a repeat of the tutorial or rules, the game only teaches you any new technology or artifact needs that come along. Which is great for someone like me who hates hearing the same things over and over. There is just enough management of staff, and visitors that if you strategize right you wont get overwhelmed or go bankrupt. The graphics are great and the interactions between the gusts and the exhibits are fun to watch. I also enjoy that I can upgrade decor and walls and floors to match the theme of the exhibit. The ability to make room templates for easy museum creation down the road is probably my favorite feature. As you move locations, it helps remove the repetitiveness on having to make the same bathroom over and over again. Overall the game feels rewarding as you move through it with out lots of repeat content as it is cozy enough to not feel like your going crazy trying to staunch issues arising. Thats why I recommend this one.

content: \n								I have completed the Career, spent a good bit of time in sandbox, and have gotten all the steam achievements. What follows is my review based on these experiences:Two Point Museum is something really special. As someone who found Two Point Hospital and Two Point Campus enjoyable but not great, I went in to Museum expecting something similar and I could not have been more surprised. You are filling Museums from 5 different main themes, and each of those main themes have their own mechanics in terms of procuring or displaying, making each theme feel unique and not just copy paste. The gameplay loop is incredibly engaging and satisfying to achieve things. To get exhibits you progress through that theme's exhibit tree, unlocking locations and sending your staff on expeditions to procure these exhibits. What really blows my mind, is that despite having about 100 hours in, finishing the career, and getting all the steam achievements, I still don't feel like I have seen even close to all there is to unlock in each exhibit theme tree. I think that Two Point Studios has made their most replayable game yet and we still don't have content updates for further expanding the sandbox mode, or DLCs yet. I have never bought a DLC for previous games but I will be buying each one for Museum day one. 10 out of 10 could not recommend Two Point Museum more!

content: \n								In the first couple of hours I was unsure of the game - not the familiar gameplay loops of Hospital and Campus.BUT after I realised that the game rewards redesigning on the fly, as you learn new mechanics, to make a more efficient museum, I started to fall in love with it.Some themes were more challenging than others. Looking at you, Supernatural and Science. But they are now becoming my favourites as they stop me training my staff in a cookie cutter way and the payoff of getting famous spirits and beating curses and efficiently crafting contraptions far outweighs the initial 'Aargh! Not the same! Not the same! No like!' at rhe beginning of their respective levels.The game is also as hard or as easy as you want it to be. Into min/maxing? Knock yourself out. Super streamline those corridors, fit in the standard rooms like a tertis puzzle and customise with freeform exhibition halls (the freeform partition walls and doorways) to get the best flow out of your museum, milking each guest for maximum buzz, knowledge and of course their endlessly deep pockets.Want to create a beautiful museum picture? You can. The balance of finance isn't tricky to work out and you're not punished for avoiding the min/max route.My major gripe at this stage is that once chapter five of each museum is complete with the museum's stories wrapped up it just 'ends'. No acknowledgement or explanation that now you get to play the museums you have built with practically infinite stars and total freedom.I also wouldn't mind an exhibiton hall room that you can build if you're not feeling super into freeform decorating. As in a room you can build in the traditional grid, complete with a door/doors that you can add decorations to to get to level 5 and then plop some exhibits in afterwards. Definitely a good game, a great entry in the series, and far more engaging than Campus was (imo).

content: \n								In the first couple of hours I was unsure of the game - not the familiar gameplay loops of Hospital and Campus.BUT after I realised that the game rewards redesigning on the fly, as you learn new mechanics, to make a more efficient museum, I started to fall in love with it.Some themes were more challenging than others. Looking at you, Supernatural and Science. But they are now becoming my favourites as they stop me training my staff in a cookie cutter way and the payoff of getting famous spirits and beating curses and efficiently crafting contraptions far outweighs the initial 'Aargh! Not the same! Not the same! No like!' at rhe beginning of their respective levels.The game is also as hard or as easy as you want it to be. Into min/maxing? Knock yourself out. Super streamline those corridors, fit in the standard rooms like a tertis puzzle and customise with freeform exhibition halls (the freeform partition walls and doorways) to get the best flow out of your museum, milking each guest for maximum buzz, knowledge and of course their endlessly deep pockets.Want to create a beautiful museum picture? You can. The balance of finance isn't tricky to work out and you're not punished for avoiding the min/max route.My major gripe at this stage is that once chapter five of each museum is complete with the museum's stories wrapped up it just 'ends'. No acknowledgement or explanation that now you get to play the museums you have built with practically infinite stars and total freedom.I also wouldn't mind an exhibiton hall room that you can build if you're not feeling super into freeform decorating. As in a room you can build in the traditional grid, complete with a door/doors that you can add decorations to to get to level 5 and then plop some exhibits in afterwards. Definitely a good game, a great entry in the series, and far more engaging than Campus was (imo).

content: \n								I think the game is good for all the reasons you'll find in the positive reviews but...There are a few buts and I can say I went quite late game according to the achievments I get.1. having to go back and forth to the same places becomes annoying. You often need to get 10 times the same item to get its full value (knowledge and quality). You need to go a lot to get building ressources and it gets annoying.2. It is also repetitive to build some items one by one when you'll need lots of them. why don't you add a way to build 5 scanners at the same time ? Robots ? And else ?3. The money is weird. Everytime you get big you'll suffer variations of budget that can be a little weird as everything seemed to be functionning a few moments before. You'll go from + 30k to -20k in one or two cycles without making big changes.Which leads to the other point :4. Zoning. Zoning seems to be an interesting system to deal with the management. But as you'll get into the system the devs built you'll be bored in 2 minutes. you have to place every single employee in zones one by one. There are no selection modes so it's a pain.5. Why would you build several museums in different spots ?The emchanics of the game offers you to build several museums and at first you understand that it gives you a lot of freedom and space to build but everytime you start a new location there are a lot of things that you have to do from scratch.You can't send any of your employees or any of your exhibitions from a museum to another and it's too bad. This would have solved the problem of having to resell the exhibition you had for the 20th time for 5000$ when it costed you more and you can't dismantle it anymore because you've reached the limit. The only things that are common are the level of the museums, the map, kudosh and decoration but it makes no real sense.You can place all the pieces of the museum in two places. I had high hopes for this game, and it was good, but it was something that was missing that I can't set my finger on.This affected me, so I had a lukewarm anticipation towards this game, and they delivered a game that has taken me by storm.  Both me and my partner can not stop playing it!The game has so much to offer from how you interact with your customers keeping buzz and happiness going, to managing the personal that can have great traits like "Donates litter to the floor".The Game really encourages you to design rooms and exhibits more. You have to watch out for thieves and have tons of expeditions to send your personal too.This was unexpected, but the expeditions make use of all personal, experts, janitors, guards and assistants, making a diverse skill set and staff much more important. In the other games, you focused the skill set so strict on some doctors and nurses and selected dedicated rooms they could work in.Here you need to mix a bit more,And the "announcer", so many laughs!I can really recommend this game. I think this game already exceeds the other Two Point games in likability and gameplay as it is on release!Just buy, build, manage and laugh!
