content: \nWacky Exhibits, Wacky Guests!The hit Two Point County franchise continues with Two Point Museum.  Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.  Everything you love about the franchise returns, including the humor, in-jokes, and Two Point Radio.The game has two modes, Campaign and Sandbox.  Campaign is story-driven and helps introduce various gameplay elements.  Sandbox is essentially the Campaign without the story and allows you to adjust certain parts of the experience before you start.  Thus, Sandbox is best attempted after exploring Campaign mode.You'll have four types of staffers with you.  Experts find exhibits and study and maintain them.  Assistants man the various cash registers - the ticket booths, gift shop, cafeteria, a couple kiosks.  Janitors clean up after litter and vomit and maintain some machinery.  New to the franchise are security guards, needed to watch for criminals as well as securely collect donations.The core gameplay is a cycle of retrieving exhibits and placing and decorating them, as this is what brings in paying guests.Each museum specializes in a theme: Prehistory, Science, Marine Life, Supernatural, Space, with a sixth theme, Botany, secondary in the Prehistory museum.  Exhibits fall into one of the broad themes, and also a subgroup.  Prehistory contains large skeletons as well as smaller fossils, frozen items, and some ancient mysteries.  Botany contains various types of interesting flora.Experts specialize in one of the broad themes.  You send them on expeditions to bring back exhibits via the convenient helicopter parked out back.Each museum gets its own expedition map, but once you unlock locations on other maps, you can freely go to them and pick up exhibits from other themes.  There's also some overlap, as plants are found in several maps and so are dino bones.Each location has specific requirements for expeditions.  First of all, they have to be unlocked, either through the storyline or by reaching certain objectives.  Sandbox mode annoyed me by not carrying over locations unlocked in Campaign to Sandbox.Once unlocked, expeditions to locations have some minimum requirements for the team you send.  Early locations require just one expert.  Later locations ask for two experts, sometimes from different themes, as well as other staffers.  Assistants are like college students helping their professor.  Janitors are needed for their mechanical expertise.  Guards protect valuable cargo.Expeditions are adventurous, and events both good and bad can happen.  This is represented by a few event cards for each location.  Expeditions can find shortcuts or get delayed, or find or lose money.Or something happens to a team member.  Injury, illness, and what the game calls "MIA" can happen.  But the last one is less "missing in action" and more just a polite way of saying "dead," to judge from the events that trigger it and the fact that the unfortunate soul is deleted from your payroll.But not to worry, as there are ways to avoid or mitigate most of the events.  Some bad events happen only at certain times of the year.  Some are cancelled by the total level of your team.Some can be cancelled by cargo items.  Expeditions can carry just one cargo item a trip.  Three are infinite-use, including a first aid kit that takes care of one injury card, but most are one-use items that have to made by a Janitor in a Workshop, such as plant camouflage to sneak past danger.Some locations are one-visit obstructions to clear.  One of the cargo items is a drill to remove pesky rock in the way.Fortunately, none of the events make you lose an exhibit and come away empty-handed.If you're deathly allergic to gacha systems, you'll hate this next part, but it's a very fair gacha system.Locations have one to five different possibilities to find, and exhibits have different rarities.  You will always get one of these, and the "random" roll feels mostly weighted to finding something new.  Even the rarest item can be found in a few trips.Exhibits also have item quality.  Your experts are not fools and know to bring back at least a halfway decent specimen, so the lowest quality is Average.  Top quality is Pristine.There is an easy way and a hard way to get Pristine exhibits.  Easy is to get multi-part exhibits such as large skeletons.  You always find the base first, and pieces to fill it out.  As the exhibit is filled in, quality rises.  A full exhibit instantly becomes Pristine.The hard way, for one-piece exhibits, is by surveying the location.  Each trip gives you more info on a location.  The better a location is surveyed, the easier it is for a team to find that perfect specimen.  You can speed up surveying by going on longer trips and taking a certain cargo item.But you aren't done once you place exhibits, as they have both Buzz and Knowledge.  Buzz excites most guests and is influenced by item quality and the decor around it.  Exhibits also have Buzz Bonuses, a bit of synergy with some piece it wants near it.  Annoyingly, there's different bonuses for different items of the same type and quality exhibit.Knowledge is found by an Expert deconstructing a spare exhibit in an Analysis room, and is displayed on info stands near exhibits.  Some guests, like the Professors, are more excited by Knowledge than Buzz.Criminals cause mischief in your museums.  Vandals just make your Experts and Janitors clean up the place.  Thieves will steal exhibits.  But your security team, including cameras and a guard watching their feeds, can spot them before they strike.  They also have a chance to catch successful thieves and instantly return exhibits.  Thieves who leave the map with an exhibit might eventually ransom it for a premium over sale price.You make money via several sources, ticket sales, cafeteria, gift shop.  You can set prices on most things individually, so you can have cheap tickets and gouge guests at the gift shop, or vice versa.But the main way to gain money is through donations.  Excited guests will happily donate to donation boxes near favorite exhibits.  Security guards collect that money.  This means that money can flow a bit annoyingly inconsistent month to month.Staff wages and item maintenance and ransoms are automatically taken out of your account, so you can fall into negative figures, which prevents you from buying new items, or expeditions or hiring new staff.The game absolutely bends over backwards to prevent you from an unplayable game due to debt.  Fall into debt and the game reminds you of the various ways to save money from firing staff to raising prices to taking out a loan.  Once again, you get three different banks with different interest rates and max loans.Fall further, and the game rescues from bankruptcy - but at a cost.  You'll have to choose a couple exhibits to lose to repossession.  Debts to banks are wiped clean and you gain some instant cash, but banks will refuse to lend to you until you reach certain milestones.Building is fairly easy.  The same build engine from Two Point Campus returns, with the ability to save room templates and copy rooms.  You still can't join two buildings on the same plot, but you can demolish the entire museum, send exhibits to storage, and rebuild.And, of course, the beloved world-building of Two Point Radio continues.  DJs Sir Nigel, Ricky, and Harrison return, along with a new hostess, Hayley.  So does the very British humor of the series.  People, items, and locations from the first two games are mentioned or return.Two Point Museum is a solid entry in the series and worth the price of admission.

content: \nWacky Exhibits, Wacky Guests!The hit Two Point County franchise continues with Two Point Museum.  Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.  Everything you love about the franchise returns, including the humor, in-jokes, and Two Point Radio.The game has two modes, Campaign and Sandbox.  Campaign is story-driven and helps introduce various gameplay elements.  Sandbox is essentially the Campaign without the story and allows you to adjust certain parts of the experience before you start.  Thus, Sandbox is best attempted after exploring Campaign mode.You'll have four types of staffers with you.  Experts find exhibits and study and maintain them.  Assistants man the various cash registers - the ticket booths, gift shop, cafeteria, a couple kiosks.  Janitors clean up after litter and vomit and maintain some machinery.  New to the franchise are security guards, needed to watch for criminals as well as securely collect donations.The core gameplay is a cycle of retrieving exhibits and placing and decorating them, as this is what brings in paying guests.Each museum specializes in a theme: Prehistory, Science, Marine Life, Supernatural, Space, with a sixth theme, Botany, secondary in the Prehistory museum.  Exhibits fall into one of the broad themes, and also a subgroup.  Prehistory contains large skeletons as well as smaller fossils, frozen items, and some ancient mysteries.  Botany contains various types of interesting flora.Experts specialize in one of the broad themes.  You send them on expeditions to bring back exhibits via the convenient helicopter parked out back.Each museum gets its own expedition map, but once you unlock locations on other maps, you can freely go to them and pick up exhibits from other themes.  There's also some overlap, as plants are found in several maps and so are dino bones.Each location has specific requirements for expeditions.  First of all, they have to be unlocked, either through the storyline or by reaching certain objectives.  Sandbox mode annoyed me by not carrying over locations unlocked in Campaign to Sandbox.Once unlocked, expeditions to locations have some minimum requirements for the team you send.  Early locations require just one expert.  Later locations ask for two experts, sometimes from different themes, as well as other staffers.  Assistants are like college students helping their professor.  Janitors are needed for their mechanical expertise.  Guards protect valuable cargo.Expeditions are adventurous, and events both good and bad can happen.  This is represented by a few event cards for each location.  Expeditions can find shortcuts or get delayed, or find or lose money.Or something happens to a team member.  Injury, illness, and what the game calls "MIA" can happen.  But the last one is less "missing in action" and more just a polite way of saying "dead," to judge from the events that trigger it and the fact that the unfortunate soul is deleted from your payroll.But not to worry, as there are ways to avoid or mitigate most of the events.  Some bad events happen only at certain times of the year.  Some are cancelled by the total level of your team.Some can be cancelled by cargo items.  Expeditions can carry just one cargo item a trip.  Three are infinite-use, including a first aid kit that takes care of one injury card, but most are one-use items that have to made by a Janitor in a Workshop, such as plant camouflage to sneak past danger.Some locations are one-visit obstructions to clear.  One of the cargo items is a drill to remove pesky rock in the way.Fortunately, none of the events make you lose an exhibit and come away empty-handed.If you're deathly allergic to gacha systems, you'll hate this next part, but it's a very fair gacha system.Locations have one to five different possibilities to find, and exhibits have different rarities.  You will always get one of these, and the "random" roll feels mostly weighted to finding something new.  Even the rarest item can be found in a few trips.Exhibits also have item quality.  Your experts are not fools and know to bring back at least a halfway decent specimen, so the lowest quality is Average.  Top quality is Pristine.There is an easy way and a hard way to get Pristine exhibits.  Easy is to get multi-part exhibits such as large skeletons.  You always find the base first, and pieces to fill it out.  As the exhibit is filled in, quality rises.  A full exhibit instantly becomes Pristine.The hard way, for one-piece exhibits, is by surveying the location.  Each trip gives you more info on a location.  The better a location is surveyed, the easier it is for a team to find that perfect specimen.  You can speed up surveying by going on longer trips and taking a certain cargo item.But you aren't done once you place exhibits, as they have both Buzz and Knowledge.  Buzz excites most guests and is influenced by item quality and the decor around it.  Exhibits also have Buzz Bonuses, a bit of synergy with some piece it wants near it.  Annoyingly, there's different bonuses for different items of the same type and quality exhibit.Knowledge is found by an Expert deconstructing a spare exhibit in an Analysis room, and is displayed on info stands near exhibits.  Some guests, like the Professors, are more excited by Knowledge than Buzz.Criminals cause mischief in your museums.  Vandals just make your Experts and Janitors clean up the place.  Thieves will steal exhibits.  But your security team, including cameras and a guard watching their feeds, can spot them before they strike.  They also have a chance to catch successful thieves and instantly return exhibits.  Thieves who leave the map with an exhibit might eventually ransom it for a premium over sale price.You make money via several sources, ticket sales, cafeteria, gift shop.  You can set prices on most things individually, so you can have cheap tickets and gouge guests at the gift shop, or vice versa.But the main way to gain money is through donations.  Excited guests will happily donate to donation boxes near favorite exhibits.  Security guards collect that money.  This means that money can flow a bit annoyingly inconsistent month to month.Staff wages and item maintenance and ransoms are automatically taken out of your account, so you can fall into negative figures, which prevents you from buying new items, or expeditions or hiring new staff.The game absolutely bends over backwards to prevent you from an unplayable game due to debt.  Fall into debt and the game reminds you of the various ways to save money from firing staff to raising prices to taking out a loan.  Once again, you get three different banks with different interest rates and max loans.Fall further, and the game rescues from bankruptcy - but at a cost.  You'll have to choose a couple exhibits to lose to repossession.  Debts to banks are wiped clean and you gain some instant cash, but banks will refuse to lend to you until you reach certain milestones.Building is fairly easy.  The same build engine from Two Point Campus returns, with the ability to save room templates and copy rooms.  You still can't join two buildings on the same plot, but you can demolish the entire museum, send exhibits to storage, and rebuild.And, of course, the beloved world-building of Two Point Radio continues.  DJs Sir Nigel, Ricky, and Harrison return, along with a new hostess, Hayley.  So does the very British humor of the series.  People, items, and locations from the first two games are mentioned or return.Two Point Museum is a solid entry in the series and worth the price of admission.

content: \nWacky Exhibits, Wacky Guests!The hit Two Point County franchise continues with Two Point Museum.  Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.  Everything you love about the franchise returns, including the humor, in-jokes, and Two Point Radio.The game has two modes, Campaign and Sandbox.  Campaign is story-driven and helps introduce various gameplay elements.  Sandbox is essentially the Campaign without the story and allows you to adjust certain parts of the experience before you start.  Thus, Sandbox is best attempted after exploring Campaign mode.You'll have four types of staffers with you.  Experts find exhibits and study and maintain them.  Assistants man the various cash registers - the ticket booths, gift shop, cafeteria, a couple kiosks.  Janitors clean up after litter and vomit and maintain some machinery.  New to the franchise are security guards, needed to watch for criminals as well as securely collect donations.The core gameplay is a cycle of retrieving exhibits and placing and decorating them, as this is what brings in paying guests.Each museum specializes in a theme: Prehistory, Science, Marine Life, Supernatural, Space, with a sixth theme, Botany, secondary in the Prehistory museum.  Exhibits fall into one of the broad themes, and also a subgroup.  Prehistory contains large skeletons as well as smaller fossils, frozen items, and some ancient mysteries.  Botany contains various types of interesting flora.Experts specialize in one of the broad themes.  You send them on expeditions to bring back exhibits via the convenient helicopter parked out back.Each museum gets its own expedition map, but once you unlock locations on other maps, you can freely go to them and pick up exhibits from other themes.  There's also some overlap, as plants are found in several maps and so are dino bones.Each location has specific requirements for expeditions.  First of all, they have to be unlocked, either through the storyline or by reaching certain objectives.  Sandbox mode annoyed me by not carrying over locations unlocked in Campaign to Sandbox.Once unlocked, expeditions to locations have some minimum requirements for the team you send.  Early locations require just one expert.  Later locations ask for two experts, sometimes from different themes, as well as other staffers.  Assistants are like college students helping their professor.  Janitors are needed for their mechanical expertise.  Guards protect valuable cargo.Expeditions are adventurous, and events both good and bad can happen.  This is represented by a few event cards for each location.  Expeditions can find shortcuts or get delayed, or find or lose money.Or something happens to a team member.  Injury, illness, and what the game calls "MIA" can happen.  But the last one is less "missing in action" and more just a polite way of saying "dead," to judge from the events that trigger it and the fact that the unfortunate soul is deleted from your payroll.But not to worry, as there are ways to avoid or mitigate most of the events.  Some bad events happen only at certain times of the year.  Some are cancelled by the total level of your team.Some can be cancelled by cargo items.  Expeditions can carry just one cargo item a trip.  Three are infinite-use, including a first aid kit that takes care of one injury card, but most are one-use items that have to made by a Janitor in a Workshop, such as plant camouflage to sneak past danger.Some locations are one-visit obstructions to clear.  One of the cargo items is a drill to remove pesky rock in the way.Fortunately, none of the events make you lose an exhibit and come away empty-handed.If you're deathly allergic to gacha systems, you'll hate this next part, but it's a very fair gacha system.Locations have one to five different possibilities to find, and exhibits have different rarities.  You will always get one of these, and the "random" roll feels mostly weighted to finding something new.  Even the rarest item can be found in a few trips.Exhibits also have item quality.  Your experts are not fools and know to bring back at least a halfway decent specimen, so the lowest quality is Average.  Top quality is Pristine.There is an easy way and a hard way to get Pristine exhibits.  Easy is to get multi-part exhibits such as large skeletons.  You always find the base first, and pieces to fill it out.  As the exhibit is filled in, quality rises.  A full exhibit instantly becomes Pristine.The hard way, for one-piece exhibits, is by surveying the location.  Each trip gives you more info on a location.  The better a location is surveyed, the easier it is for a team to find that perfect specimen.  You can speed up surveying by going on longer trips and taking a certain cargo item.But you aren't done once you place exhibits, as they have both Buzz and Knowledge.  Buzz excites most guests and is influenced by item quality and the decor around it.  Exhibits also have Buzz Bonuses, a bit of synergy with some piece it wants near it.  Annoyingly, there's different bonuses for different items of the same type and quality exhibit.Knowledge is found by an Expert deconstructing a spare exhibit in an Analysis room, and is displayed on info stands near exhibits.  Some guests, like the Professors, are more excited by Knowledge than Buzz.Criminals cause mischief in your museums.  Vandals just make your Experts and Janitors clean up the place.  Thieves will steal exhibits.  But your security team, including cameras and a guard watching their feeds, can spot them before they strike.  They also have a chance to catch successful thieves and instantly return exhibits.  Thieves who leave the map with an exhibit might eventually ransom it for a premium over sale price.You make money via several sources, ticket sales, cafeteria, gift shop.  You can set prices on most things individually, so you can have cheap tickets and gouge guests at the gift shop, or vice versa.But the main way to gain money is through donations.  Excited guests will happily donate to donation boxes near favorite exhibits.  Security guards collect that money.  This means that money can flow a bit annoyingly inconsistent month to month.Staff wages and item maintenance and ransoms are automatically taken out of your account, so you can fall into negative figures, which prevents you from buying new items, or expeditions or hiring new staff.The game absolutely bends over backwards to prevent you from an unplayable game due to debt.  Fall into debt and the game reminds you of the various ways to save money from firing staff to raising prices to taking out a loan.  Once again, you get three different banks with different interest rates and max loans.Fall further, and the game rescues from bankruptcy - but at a cost.  You'll have to choose a couple exhibits to lose to repossession.  Debts to banks are wiped clean and you gain some instant cash, but banks will refuse to lend to you until you reach certain milestones.Building is fairly easy.  The same build engine from Two Point Campus returns, with the ability to save room templates and copy rooms.  You still can't join two buildings on the same plot, but you can demolish the entire museum, send exhibits to storage, and rebuild.And, of course, the beloved world-building of Two Point Radio continues.  DJs Sir Nigel, Ricky, and Harrison return, along with a new hostess, Hayley.  So does the very British humor of the series.  People, items, and locations from the first two games are mentioned or return.Two Point Museum is a solid entry in the series and worth the price of admission.

Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.  Everything you love about the franchise returns, including the humor, in-jokes, and Two Point Radio.The game has two modes, Campaign and Sandbox.  Campaign is story-driven and helps introduce various gameplay elements.  Sandbox is essentially the Campaign without the story and allows you to adjust certain parts of the experience before you start.  Thus, Sandbox is best attempted after exploring Campaign mode.You'll have four types of staffers with you.  Experts find exhibits and study and maintain them.  Assistants man the various cash registers - the ticket booths, gift shop, cafeteria, a couple kiosks.  Janitors clean up after litter and vomit and maintain some machinery.  New to the franchise are security guards, needed to watch for criminals as well as securely collect donations.The core gameplay is a cycle of retrieving exhibits and placing and decorating them, as this is what brings in paying guests.Each museum specializes in a theme: Prehistory, Science, Marine Life, Supernatural, Space, with a sixth theme, Botany, secondary in the Prehistory museum.  Exhibits fall into one of the broad themes, and also a subgroup.  Prehistory contains large skeletons as well as smaller fossils, frozen items, and some ancient mysteries.  Botany contains various types of interesting flora.Experts specialize in one of the broad themes.  You send them on expeditions to bring back exhibits via the convenient helicopter parked out back.Each museum gets its own expedition map, but once you unlock locations on other maps, you can freely go to them and pick up exhibits from other themes.  There's also some overlap, as plants are found in several maps and so are dino bones.Each location has specific requirements for expeditions.  First of all, they have to be unlocked, either through the storyline or by reaching certain objectives.  Sandbox mode annoyed me by not carrying over locations unlocked in Campaign to Sandbox.Once unlocked, expeditions to locations have some minimum requirements for the team you send.  Early locations require just one expert.  Later locations ask for two experts, sometimes from different themes, as well as other staffers.  Assistants are like college students helping their professor.  Janitors are needed for their mechanical expertise.  Guards protect valuable cargo.Expeditions are adventurous, and events both good and bad can happen.  This is represented by a few event cards for each location.  Expeditions can find shortcuts or get delayed, or find or lose money.Or something happens to a team member.  Injury, illness, and what the game calls "MIA" can happen.  But the last one is less "missing in action" and more just a polite way of saying "dead," to judge from the events that trigger it and the fact that the unfortunate soul is deleted from your payroll.But not to worry, as there are ways to avoid or mitigate most of the events.  Some bad events happen only at certain times of the year.  Some are cancelled by the total level of your team.Some can be cancelled by cargo items.  Expeditions can carry just one cargo item a trip.  Three are infinite-use, including a first aid kit that takes care of one injury card, but most are one-use items that have to made by a Janitor in a Workshop, such as plant camouflage to sneak past danger.Some locations are one-visit obstructions to clear.  One of the cargo items is a drill to remove pesky rock in the way.Fortunately, none of the events make you lose an exhibit and come away empty-handed.If you're deathly allergic to gacha systems, you'll hate this next part, but it's a very fair gacha system.Locations have one to five different possibilities to find, and exhibits have different rarities.  You will always get one of these, and the "random" roll feels mostly weighted to finding something new.  Even the rarest item can be found in a few trips.Exhibits also have item quality.  Your experts are not fools and know to bring back at least a halfway decent specimen, so the lowest quality is Average.  Top quality is Pristine.There is an easy way and a hard way to get Pristine exhibits.  Easy is to get multi-part exhibits such as large skeletons.  You always find the base first, and pieces to fill it out.  As the exhibit is filled in, quality rises.  A full exhibit instantly becomes Pristine.The hard way, for one-piece exhibits, is by surveying the location.  Each trip gives you more info on a location.  The better a location is surveyed, the easier it is for a team to find that perfect specimen.  You can speed up surveying by going on longer trips and taking a certain cargo item.But you aren't done once you place exhibits, as they have both Buzz and Knowledge.  Buzz excites most guests and is influenced by item quality and the decor around it.  Exhibits also have Buzz Bonuses, a bit of synergy with some piece it wants near it.  Annoyingly, there's different bonuses for different items of the same type and quality exhibit.Knowledge is found by an Expert deconstructing a spare exhibit in an Analysis room, and is displayed on info stands near exhibits.  Some guests, like the Professors, are more excited by Knowledge than Buzz.Criminals cause mischief in your museums.  Vandals just make your Experts and Janitors clean up the place.  Thieves will steal exhibits.  But your security team, including cameras and a guard watching their feeds, can spot them before they strike.  They also have a chance to catch successful thieves and instantly return exhibits.  Thieves who leave the map with an exhibit might eventually ransom it for a premium over sale price.You make money via several sources, ticket sales, cafeteria, gift shop.  You can set prices on most things individually, so you can have cheap tickets and gouge guests at the gift shop, or vice versa.But the main way to gain money is through donations.  Excited guests will happily donate to donation boxes near favorite exhibits.  Security guards collect that money.  This means that money can flow a bit annoyingly inconsistent month to month.Staff wages and item maintenance and ransoms are automatically taken out of your account, so you can fall into negative figures, which prevents you from buying new items, or expeditions or hiring new staff.The game absolutely bends over backwards to prevent you from an unplayable game due to debt.  Fall into debt and the game reminds you of the various ways to save money from firing staff to raising prices to taking out a loan.  Once again, you get three different banks with different interest rates and max loans.Fall further, and the game rescues from bankruptcy - but at a cost.  You'll have to choose a couple exhibits to lose to repossession.  Debts to banks are wiped clean and you gain some instant cash, but banks will refuse to lend to you until you reach certain milestones.Building is fairly easy.  The same build engine from Two Point Campus returns, with the ability to save room templates and copy rooms.  You still can't join two buildings on the same plot, but you can demolish the entire museum, send exhibits to storage, and rebuild.And, of course, the beloved world-building of Two Point Radio continues.  DJs Sir Nigel, Ricky, and Harrison return, along with a new hostess, Hayley.  So does the very British humor of the series.  People, items, and locations from the first two games are mentioned or return.Two Point Museum is a solid entry in the series and worth the price of admission.

content: \nWacky Exhibits, Wacky Guests!The hit Two Point County franchise continues with Two Point Museum.  Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.  Everything you love about the franchise returns, including the humor, in-jokes, and Two Point Radio.The game has two modes, Campaign and Sandbox.  Campaign is story-driven and helps introduce various gameplay elements.  Sandbox is essentially the Campaign without the story and allows you to adjust certain parts of the experience before you start.  Thus, Sandbox is best attempted after exploring Campaign mode.You'll have four types of staffers with you.  Experts find exhibits and study and maintain them.  Assistants man the various cash registers - the ticket booths, gift shop, cafeteria, a couple kiosks.  Janitors clean up after litter and vomit and maintain some machinery.  New to the franchise are security guards, needed to watch for criminals as well as securely collect donations.The core gameplay is a cycle of retrieving exhibits and placing and decorating them, as this is what brings in paying guests.Each museum specializes in a theme: Prehistory, Science, Marine Life, Supernatural, Space, with a sixth theme, Botany, secondary in the Prehistory museum.  Exhibits fall into one of the broad themes, and also a subgroup.  Prehistory contains large skeletons as well as smaller fossils, frozen items, and some ancient mysteries.  Botany contains various types of interesting flora.Experts specialize in one of the broad themes.  You send them on expeditions to bring back exhibits via the convenient helicopter parked out back.Each museum gets its own expedition map, but once you unlock locations on other maps, you can freely go to them and pick up exhibits from other themes.  There's also some overlap, as plants are found in several maps and so are dino bones.Each location has specific requirements for expeditions.  First of all, they have to be unlocked, either through the storyline or by reaching certain objectives.  Sandbox mode annoyed me by not carrying over locations unlocked in Campaign to Sandbox.Once unlocked, expeditions to locations have some minimum requirements for the team you send.  Early locations require just one expert.  Later locations ask for two experts, sometimes from different themes, as well as other staffers.  Assistants are like college students helping their professor.  Janitors are needed for their mechanical expertise.  Guards protect valuable cargo.Expeditions are adventurous, and events both good and bad can happen.  This is represented by a few event cards for each location.  Expeditions can find shortcuts or get delayed, or find or lose money.Or something happens to a team member.  Injury, illness, and what the game calls "MIA" can happen.  But the last one is less "missing in action" and more just a polite way of saying "dead," to judge from the events that trigger it and the fact that the unfortunate soul is deleted from your payroll.But not to worry, as there are ways to avoid or mitigate most of the events.  Some bad events happen only at certain times of the year.  Some are cancelled by the total level of your team.Some can be cancelled by cargo items.  Expeditions can carry just one cargo item a trip.  Three are infinite-use, including a first aid kit that takes care of one injury card, but most are one-use items that have to made by a Janitor in a Workshop, such as plant camouflage to sneak past danger.Some locations are one-visit obstructions to clear.  One of the cargo items is a drill to remove pesky rock in the way.Fortunately, none of the events make you lose an exhibit and come away empty-handed.If you're deathly allergic to gacha systems, you'll hate this next part, but it's a very fair gacha system.Locations have one to five different possibilities to find, and exhibits have different rarities.  You will always get one of these, and the "random" roll feels mostly weighted to finding something new.  Even the rarest item can be found in a few trips.Exhibits also have item quality.  Your experts are not fools and know to bring back at least a halfway decent specimen, so the lowest quality is Average.  Top quality is Pristine.There is an easy way and a hard way to get Pristine exhibits.  Easy is to get multi-part exhibits such as large skeletons.  You always find the base first, and pieces to fill it out.  As the exhibit is filled in, quality rises.  A full exhibit instantly becomes Pristine.The hard way, for one-piece exhibits, is by surveying the location.  Each trip gives you more info on a location.  The better a location is surveyed, the easier it is for a team to find that perfect specimen.  You can speed up surveying by going on longer trips and taking a certain cargo item.But you aren't done once you place exhibits, as they have both Buzz and Knowledge.  Buzz excites most guests and is influenced by item quality and the decor around it.  Exhibits also have Buzz Bonuses, a bit of synergy with some piece it wants near it.  Annoyingly, there's different bonuses for different items of the same type and quality exhibit.Knowledge is found by an Expert deconstructing a spare exhibit in an Analysis room, and is displayed on info stands near exhibits.  Some guests, like the Professors, are more excited by Knowledge than Buzz.Criminals cause mischief in your museums.  Vandals just make your Experts and Janitors clean up the place.  Thieves will steal exhibits.  But your security team, including cameras and a guard watching their feeds, can spot them before they strike.  They also have a chance to catch successful thieves and instantly return exhibits.  Thieves who leave the map with an exhibit might eventually ransom it for a premium over sale price.You make money via several sources, ticket sales, cafeteria, gift shop.  You can set prices on most things individually, so you can have cheap tickets and gouge guests at the gift shop, or vice versa.But the main way to gain money is through donations.  Excited guests will happily donate to donation boxes near favorite exhibits.  Security guards collect that money.  This means that money can flow a bit annoyingly inconsistent month to month.Staff wages and item maintenance and ransoms are automatically taken out of your account, so you can fall into negative figures, which prevents you from buying new items, or expeditions or hiring new staff.The game absolutely bends over backwards to prevent you from an unplayable game due to debt.  Fall into debt and the game reminds you of the various ways to save money from firing staff to raising prices to taking out a loan.  Once again, you get three different banks with different interest rates and max loans.Fall further, and the game rescues from bankruptcy - but at a cost.  You'll have to choose a couple exhibits to lose to repossession.  Debts to banks are wiped clean and you gain some instant cash, but banks will refuse to lend to you until you reach certain milestones.Building is fairly easy.  The same build engine from Two Point Campus returns, with the ability to save room templates and copy rooms.  You still can't join two buildings on the same plot, but you can demolish the entire museum, send exhibits to storage, and rebuild.And, of course, the beloved world-building of Two Point Radio continues.  DJs Sir Nigel, Ricky, and Harrison return, along with a new hostess, Hayley.  So does the very British humor of the series.  People, items, and locations from the first two games are mentioned or return.Two Point Museum is a solid entry in the series and worth the price of admission.

content: \nWacky Exhibits, Wacky Guests!The hit Two Point County franchise continues with Two Point Museum.  Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.  Everything you love about the franchise returns, including the humor, in-jokes, and Two Point Radio.The game has two modes, Campaign and Sandbox.  Campaign is story-driven and helps introduce various gameplay elements.  Sandbox is essentially the Campaign without the story and allows you to adjust certain parts of the experience before you start.  Thus, Sandbox is best attempted after exploring Campaign mode.You'll have four types of staffers with you.  Experts find exhibits and study and maintain them.  Assistants man the various cash registers - the ticket booths, gift shop, cafeteria, a couple kiosks.  Janitors clean up after litter and vomit and maintain some machinery.  New to the franchise are security guards, needed to watch for criminals as well as securely collect donations.The core gameplay is a cycle of retrieving exhibits and placing and decorating them, as this is what brings in paying guests.Each museum specializes in a theme: Prehistory, Science, Marine Life, Supernatural, Space, with a sixth theme, Botany, secondary in the Prehistory museum.  Exhibits fall into one of the broad themes, and also a subgroup.  Prehistory contains large skeletons as well as smaller fossils, frozen items, and some ancient mysteries.  Botany contains various types of interesting flora.Experts specialize in one of the broad themes.  You send them on expeditions to bring back exhibits via the convenient helicopter parked out back.Each museum gets its own expedition map, but once you unlock locations on other maps, you can freely go to them and pick up exhibits from other themes.  There's also some overlap, as plants are found in several maps and so are dino bones.Each location has specific requirements for expeditions.  First of all, they have to be unlocked, either through the storyline or by reaching certain objectives.  Sandbox mode annoyed me by not carrying over locations unlocked in Campaign to Sandbox.Once unlocked, expeditions to locations have some minimum requirements for the team you send.  Early locations require just one expert.  Later locations ask for two experts, sometimes from different themes, as well as other staffers.  Assistants are like college students helping their professor.  Janitors are needed for their mechanical expertise.  Guards protect valuable cargo.Expeditions are adventurous, and events both good and bad can happen.  This is represented by a few event cards for each location.  Expeditions can find shortcuts or get delayed, or find or lose money.Or something happens to a team member.  Injury, illness, and what the game calls "MIA" can happen.  But the last one is less "missing in action" and more just a polite way of saying "dead," to judge from the events that trigger it and the fact that the unfortunate soul is deleted from your payroll.But not to worry, as there are ways to avoid or mitigate most of the events.  Some bad events happen only at certain times of the year.  Some are cancelled by the total level of your team.Some can be cancelled by cargo items.  Expeditions can carry just one cargo item a trip.  Three are infinite-use, including a first aid kit that takes care of one injury card, but most are one-use items that have to made by a Janitor in a Workshop, such as plant camouflage to sneak past danger.Some locations are one-visit obstructions to clear.  One of the cargo items is a drill to remove pesky rock in the way.Fortunately, none of the events make you lose an exhibit and come away empty-handed.If you're deathly allergic to gacha systems, you'll hate this next part, but it's a very fair gacha system.Locations have one to five different possibilities to find, and exhibits have different rarities.  You will always get one of these, and the "random" roll feels mostly weighted to finding something new.  Even the rarest item can be found in a few trips.Exhibits also have item quality.  Your experts are not fools and know to bring back at least a halfway decent specimen, so the lowest quality is Average.  Top quality is Pristine.There is an easy way and a hard way to get Pristine exhibits.  Easy is to get multi-part exhibits such as large skeletons.  You always find the base first, and pieces to fill it out.  As the exhibit is filled in, quality rises.  A full exhibit instantly becomes Pristine.The hard way, for one-piece exhibits, is by surveying the location.  Each trip gives you more info on a location.  The better a location is surveyed, the easier it is for a team to find that perfect specimen.  You can speed up surveying by going on longer trips and taking a certain cargo item.But you aren't done once you place exhibits, as they have both Buzz and Knowledge.  Buzz excites most guests and is influenced by item quality and the decor around it.  Exhibits also have Buzz Bonuses, a bit of synergy with some piece it wants near it.  Annoyingly, there's different bonuses for different items of the same type and quality exhibit.Knowledge is found by an Expert deconstructing a spare exhibit in an Analysis room, and is displayed on info stands near exhibits.  Some guests, like the Professors, are more excited by Knowledge than Buzz.Criminals cause mischief in your museums.  Vandals just make your Experts and Janitors clean up the place.  Thieves will steal exhibits.  But your security team, including cameras and a guard watching their feeds, can spot them before they strike.  They also have a chance to catch successful thieves and instantly return exhibits.  Thieves who leave the map with an exhibit might eventually ransom it for a premium over sale price.You make money via several sources, ticket sales, cafeteria, gift shop.  You can set prices on most things individually, so you can have cheap tickets and gouge guests at the gift shop, or vice versa.But the main way to gain money is through donations.  Excited guests will happily donate to donation boxes near favorite exhibits.  Security guards collect that money.  This means that money can flow a bit annoyingly inconsistent month to month.Staff wages and item maintenance and ransoms are automatically taken out of your account, so you can fall into negative figures, which prevents you from buying new items, or expeditions or hiring new staff.The game absolutely bends over backwards to prevent you from an unplayable game due to debt.  Fall into debt and the game reminds you of the various ways to save money from firing staff to raising prices to taking out a loan.  Once again, you get three different banks with different interest rates and max loans.Fall further, and the game rescues from bankruptcy - but at a cost.  You'll have to choose a couple exhibits to lose to repossession.  Debts to banks are wiped clean and you gain some instant cash, but banks will refuse to lend to you until you reach certain milestones.Building is fairly easy.  The same build engine from Two Point Campus returns, with the ability to save room templates and copy rooms.  You still can't join two buildings on the same plot, but you can demolish the entire museum, send exhibits to storage, and rebuild.And, of course, the beloved world-building of Two Point Radio continues.  DJs Sir Nigel, Ricky, and Harrison return, along with a new hostess, Hayley.  So does the very British humor of the series.  People, items, and locations from the first two games are mentioned or return.Two Point Museum is a solid entry in the series and worth the price of admission.

content: \nWacky Exhibits, Wacky Guests!The hit Two Point County franchise continues with Two Point Museum.  Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.  Everything you love about the franchise returns, including the humor, in-jokes, and Two Point Radio.The game has two modes, Campaign and Sandbox.  Campaign is story-driven and helps introduce various gameplay elements.  Sandbox is essentially the Campaign without the story and allows you to adjust certain parts of the experience before you start.  Thus, Sandbox is best attempted after exploring Campaign mode.You'll have four types of staffers with you.  Experts find exhibits and study and maintain them.  Assistants man the various cash registers - the ticket booths, gift shop, cafeteria, a couple kiosks.  Janitors clean up after litter and vomit and maintain some machinery.  New to the franchise are security guards, needed to watch for criminals as well as securely collect donations.The core gameplay is a cycle of retrieving exhibits and placing and decorating them, as this is what brings in paying guests.Each museum specializes in a theme: Prehistory, Science, Marine Life, Supernatural, Space, with a sixth theme, Botany, secondary in the Prehistory museum.  Exhibits fall into one of the broad themes, and also a subgroup.  Prehistory contains large skeletons as well as smaller fossils, frozen items, and some ancient mysteries.  Botany contains various types of interesting flora.Experts specialize in one of the broad themes.  You send them on expeditions to bring back exhibits via the convenient helicopter parked out back.Each museum gets its own expedition map, but once you unlock locations on other maps, you can freely go to them and pick up exhibits from other themes.  There's also some overlap, as plants are found in several maps and so are dino bones.Each location has specific requirements for expeditions.  First of all, they have to be unlocked, either through the storyline or by reaching certain objectives.  Sandbox mode annoyed me by not carrying over locations unlocked in Campaign to Sandbox.Once unlocked, expeditions to locations have some minimum requirements for the team you send.  Early locations require just one expert.  Later locations ask for two experts, sometimes from different themes, as well as other staffers.  Assistants are like college students helping their professor.  Janitors are needed for their mechanical expertise.  Guards protect valuable cargo.Expeditions are adventurous, and events both good and bad can happen.  This is represented by a few event cards for each location.  Expeditions can find shortcuts or get delayed, or find or lose money.Or something happens to a team member.  Injury, illness, and what the game calls "MIA" can happen.  But the last one is less "missing in action" and more just a polite way of saying "dead," to judge from the events that trigger it and the fact that the unfortunate soul is deleted from your payroll.But not to worry, as there are ways to avoid or mitigate most of the events.  Some bad events happen only at certain times of the year.  Some are cancelled by the total level of your team.Some can be cancelled by cargo items.  Expeditions can carry just one cargo item a trip.  Three are infinite-use, including a first aid kit that takes care of one injury card, but most are one-use items that have to made by a Janitor in a Workshop, such as plant camouflage to sneak past danger.Some locations are one-visit obstructions to clear.  One of the cargo items is a drill to remove pesky rock in the way.Fortunately, none of the events make you lose an exhibit and come away empty-handed.If you're deathly allergic to gacha systems, you'll hate this next part, but it's a very fair gacha system.Locations have one to five different possibilities to find, and exhibits have different rarities.  You will always get one of these, and the "random" roll feels mostly weighted to finding something new.  Even the rarest item can be found in a few trips.Exhibits also have item quality.  Your experts are not fools and know to bring back at least a halfway decent specimen, so the lowest quality is Average.  Top quality is Pristine.There is an easy way and a hard way to get Pristine exhibits.  Easy is to get multi-part exhibits such as large skeletons.  You always find the base first, and pieces to fill it out.  As the exhibit is filled in, quality rises.  A full exhibit instantly becomes Pristine.The hard way, for one-piece exhibits, is by surveying the location.  Each trip gives you more info on a location.  The better a location is surveyed, the easier it is for a team to find that perfect specimen.  You can speed up surveying by going on longer trips and taking a certain cargo item.But you aren't done once you place exhibits, as they have both Buzz and Knowledge.  Buzz excites most guests and is influenced by item quality and the decor around it.  Exhibits also have Buzz Bonuses, a bit of synergy with some piece it wants near it.  Annoyingly, there's different bonuses for different items of the same type and quality exhibit.Knowledge is found by an Expert deconstructing a spare exhibit in an Analysis room, and is displayed on info stands near exhibits.  Some guests, like the Professors, are more excited by Knowledge than Buzz.Criminals cause mischief in your museums.  Vandals just make your Experts and Janitors clean up the place.  Thieves will steal exhibits.  But your security team, including cameras and a guard watching their feeds, can spot them before they strike.  They also have a chance to catch successful thieves and instantly return exhibits.  Thieves who leave the map with an exhibit might eventually ransom it for a premium over sale price.You make money via several sources, ticket sales, cafeteria, gift shop.  You can set prices on most things individually, so you can have cheap tickets and gouge guests at the gift shop, or vice versa.But the main way to gain money is through donations.  Excited guests will happily donate to donation boxes near favorite exhibits.  Security guards collect that money.  This means that money can flow a bit annoyingly inconsistent month to month.Staff wages and item maintenance and ransoms are automatically taken out of your account, so you can fall into negative figures, which prevents you from buying new items, or expeditions or hiring new staff.The game absolutely bends over backwards to prevent you from an unplayable game due to debt.  Fall into debt and the game reminds you of the various ways to save money from firing staff to raising prices to taking out a loan.  Once again, you get three different banks with different interest rates and max loans.Fall further, and the game rescues from bankruptcy - but at a cost.  You'll have to choose a couple exhibits to lose to repossession.  Debts to banks are wiped clean and you gain some instant cash, but banks will refuse to lend to you until you reach certain milestones.Building is fairly easy.  The same build engine from Two Point Campus returns, with the ability to save room templates and copy rooms.  You still can't join two buildings on the same plot, but you can demolish the entire museum, send exhibits to storage, and rebuild.And, of course, the beloved world-building of Two Point Radio continues.  DJs Sir Nigel, Ricky, and Harrison return, along with a new hostess, Hayley.  So does the very British humor of the series.  People, items, and locations from the first two games are mentioned or return.Two Point Museum is a solid entry in the series and worth the price of admission.

Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.  Everything you love about the franchise returns, including the humor, in-jokes, and Two Point Radio.The game has two modes, Campaign and Sandbox.  Campaign is story-driven and helps introduce various gameplay elements.  Sandbox is essentially the Campaign without the story and allows you to adjust certain parts of the experience before you start.  Thus, Sandbox is best attempted after exploring Campaign mode.You'll have four types of staffers with you.  Experts find exhibits and study and maintain them.  Assistants man the various cash registers - the ticket booths, gift shop, cafeteria, a couple kiosks.  Janitors clean up after litter and vomit and maintain some machinery.  New to the franchise are security guards, needed to watch for criminals as well as securely collect donations.The core gameplay is a cycle of retrieving exhibits and placing and decorating them, as this is what brings in paying guests.Each museum specializes in a theme: Prehistory, Science, Marine Life, Supernatural, Space, with a sixth theme, Botany, secondary in the Prehistory museum.  Exhibits fall into one of the broad themes, and also a subgroup.  Prehistory contains large skeletons as well as smaller fossils, frozen items, and some ancient mysteries.  Botany contains various types of interesting flora.Experts specialize in one of the broad themes.  You send them on expeditions to bring back exhibits via the convenient helicopter parked out back.Each museum gets its own expedition map, but once you unlock locations on other maps, you can freely go to them and pick up exhibits from other themes.  There's also some overlap, as plants are found in several maps and so are dino bones.Each location has specific requirements for expeditions.  First of all, they have to be unlocked, either through the storyline or by reaching certain objectives.  Sandbox mode annoyed me by not carrying over locations unlocked in Campaign to Sandbox.Once unlocked, expeditions to locations have some minimum requirements for the team you send.  Early locations require just one expert.  Later locations ask for two experts, sometimes from different themes, as well as other staffers.  Assistants are like college students helping their professor.  Janitors are needed for their mechanical expertise.  Guards protect valuable cargo.Expeditions are adventurous, and events both good and bad can happen.  This is represented by a few event cards for each location.  Expeditions can find shortcuts or get delayed, or find or lose money.Or something happens to a team member.  Injury, illness, and what the game calls "MIA" can happen.  But the last one is less "missing in action" and more just a polite way of saying "dead," to judge from the events that trigger it and the fact that the unfortunate soul is deleted from your payroll.But not to worry, as there are ways to avoid or mitigate most of the events.  Some bad events happen only at certain times of the year.  Some are cancelled by the total level of your team.Some can be cancelled by cargo items.  Expeditions can carry just one cargo item a trip.  Three are infinite-use, including a first aid kit that takes care of one injury card, but most are one-use items that have to made by a Janitor in a Workshop, such as plant camouflage to sneak past danger.Some locations are one-visit obstructions to clear.  One of the cargo items is a drill to remove pesky rock in the way.Fortunately, none of the events make you lose an exhibit and come away empty-handed.If you're deathly allergic to gacha systems, you'll hate this next part, but it's a very fair gacha system.Locations have one to five different possibilities to find, and exhibits have different rarities.  You will always get one of these, and the "random" roll feels mostly weighted to finding something new.  Even the rarest item can be found in a few trips.Exhibits also have item quality.  Your experts are not fools and know to bring back at least a halfway decent specimen, so the lowest quality is Average.  Top quality is Pristine.There is an easy way and a hard way to get Pristine exhibits.  Easy is to get multi-part exhibits such as large skeletons.  You always find the base first, and pieces to fill it out.  As the exhibit is filled in, quality rises.  A full exhibit instantly becomes Pristine.The hard way, for one-piece exhibits, is by surveying the location.  Each trip gives you more info on a location.  The better a location is surveyed, the easier it is for a team to find that perfect specimen.  You can speed up surveying by going on longer trips and taking a certain cargo item.But you aren't done once you place exhibits, as they have both Buzz and Knowledge.  Buzz excites most guests and is influenced by item quality and the decor around it.  Exhibits also have Buzz Bonuses, a bit of synergy with some piece it wants near it.  Annoyingly, there's different bonuses for different items of the same type and quality exhibit.Knowledge is found by an Expert deconstructing a spare exhibit in an Analysis room, and is displayed on info stands near exhibits.  Some guests, like the Professors, are more excited by Knowledge than Buzz.Criminals cause mischief in your museums.  Vandals just make your Experts and Janitors clean up the place.  Thieves will steal exhibits.  But your security team, including cameras and a guard watching their feeds, can spot them before they strike.  They also have a chance to catch successful thieves and instantly return exhibits.  Thieves who leave the map with an exhibit might eventually ransom it for a premium over sale price.You make money via several sources, ticket sales, cafeteria, gift shop.  You can set prices on most things individually, so you can have cheap tickets and gouge guests at the gift shop, or vice versa.But the main way to gain money is through donations.  Excited guests will happily donate to donation boxes near favorite exhibits.  Security guards collect that money.  This means that money can flow a bit annoyingly inconsistent month to month.Staff wages and item maintenance and ransoms are automatically taken out of your account, so you can fall into negative figures, which prevents you from buying new items, or expeditions or hiring new staff.The game absolutely bends over backwards to prevent you from an unplayable game due to debt.  Fall into debt and the game reminds you of the various ways to save money from firing staff to raising prices to taking out a loan.  Once again, you get three different banks with different interest rates and max loans.Fall further, and the game rescues from bankruptcy - but at a cost. Debts to banks are wiped clean and you gain some instant cash, but banks will refuse to lend to you until you reach certain milestones.Building is fairly easy. You still can't join two buildings on the same plot, but you can demolish the entire museum, send exhibits to storage, and rebuild.And, of course, the beloved world-building of Two Point Radio continues. People, items, and locations from the first two games are mentioned or return.Two Point Museum is a solid entry in the series and worth the price of admission.

content: \nWacky Exhibits, Wacky Guests!The hit Two Point County franchise continues with Two Point Museum.  Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.  Everything you love about the franchise returns, including the humor, in-jokes, and Two Point Radio.The game has two modes, Campaign and Sandbox.  Campaign is story-driven and helps introduce various gameplay elements.  Sandbox is essentially the Campaign without the story and allows you to adjust certain parts of the experience before you start.  Thus, Sandbox is best attempted after exploring Campaign mode.You'll have four types of staffers with you.  Experts find exhibits and study and maintain them.  Assistants man the various cash registers - the ticket booths, gift shop, cafeteria, a couple kiosks.  Janitors clean up after litter and vomit and maintain some machinery.  New to the franchise are security guards, needed to watch for criminals as well as securely collect donations.The core gameplay is a cycle of retrieving exhibits and placing and decorating them, as this is what brings in paying guests.Each museum specializes in a theme: Prehistory, Science, Marine Life, Supernatural, Space, with a sixth theme, Botany, secondary in the Prehistory museum.  Exhibits fall into one of the broad themes, and also a subgroup.  Prehistory contains large skeletons as well as smaller fossils, frozen items, and some ancient mysteries.  Botany contains various types of interesting flora.Experts specialize in one of the broad themes.  You send them on expeditions to bring back exhibits via the convenient helicopter parked out back.Each museum gets its own expedition map, but once you unlock locations on other maps, you can freely go to them and pick up exhibits from other themes.  There's also some overlap, as plants are found in several maps and so are dino bones.Each location has specific requirements for expeditions.  First of all, they have to be unlocked, either through the storyline or by reaching certain objectives.  Sandbox mode annoyed me by not carrying over locations unlocked in Campaign to Sandbox.Once unlocked, expeditions to locations have some minimum requirements for the team you send.  Early locations require just one expert.  Later locations ask for two experts, sometimes from different themes, as well as other staffers.  Assistants are like college students helping their professor.  Janitors are needed for their mechanical expertise.  Guards protect valuable cargo.Expeditions are adventurous, and events both good and bad can happen.  This is represented by a few event cards for each location.  Expeditions can find shortcuts or get delayed, or find or lose money.Or something happens to a team member.  Injury, illness, and what the game calls "MIA" can happen.  But the last one is less "missing in action" and more just a polite way of saying "dead," to judge from the events that trigger it and the fact that the unfortunate soul is deleted from your payroll.But not to worry, as there are ways to avoid or mitigate most of the events.  Some bad events happen only at certain times of the year.  Some are cancelled by the total level of your team.Some can be cancelled by cargo items.  Expeditions can carry just one cargo item a trip.  Three are infinite-use, including a first aid kit that takes care of one injury card, but most are one-use items that have to made by a Janitor in a Workshop, such as plant camouflage to sneak past danger.Some locations are one-visit obstructions to clear.  One of the cargo items is a drill to remove pesky rock in the way.Fortunately, none of the events make you lose an exhibit and come away empty-handed.If you're deathly allergic to gacha systems, you'll hate this next part, but it's a very fair gacha system.Locations have one to five different possibilities to find, and exhibits have different rarities.  You will always get one of these, and the "random" roll feels mostly weighted to finding something new.  Even the rarest item can be found in a few trips.Exhibits also have item quality.  Your experts are not fools and know to bring back at least a halfway decent specimen, so the lowest quality is Average.  Top quality is Pristine.There is an easy way and a hard way to get Pristine exhibits.  Easy is to get multi-part exhibits such as large skeletons.  You always find the base first, and pieces to fill it out.  As the exhibit is filled in, quality rises.  A full exhibit instantly becomes Pristine.The hard way, for one-piece exhibits, is by surveying the location.  Each trip gives you more info on a location.  The better a location is surveyed, the easier it is for a team to find that perfect specimen.  You can speed up surveying by going on longer trips and taking a certain cargo item.But you aren't done once you place exhibits, as they have both Buzz and Knowledge.  Buzz excites most guests and is influenced by item quality and the decor around it.  Exhibits also have Buzz Bonuses, a bit of synergy with some piece it wants near it.  Annoyingly, there's different bonuses for different items of the same type and quality exhibit.Knowledge is found by an Expert deconstructing a spare exhibit in an Analysis room, and is displayed on info stands near exhibits.  Some guests, like the Professors, are more excited by Knowledge than Buzz.Criminals cause mischief in your museums.  Vandals just make your Experts and Janitors clean up the place.  Thieves will steal exhibits.  But your security team, including cameras and a guard watching their feeds, can spot them before they strike.  They also have a chance to catch successful thieves and instantly return exhibits.  Thieves who leave the map with an exhibit might eventually ransom it for a premium over sale price.You make money via several sources, ticket sales, cafeteria, gift shop.  You can set prices on most things individually, so you can have cheap tickets and gouge guests at the gift shop, or vice versa.But the main way to gain money is through donations.  Excited guests will happily donate to donation boxes near favorite exhibits.  Security guards collect that money.  This means that money can flow a bit annoyingly inconsistent month to month.Staff wages and item maintenance and ransoms are automatically taken out of your account, so you can fall into negative figures, which prevents you from buying new items, or expeditions or hiring new staff.The game absolutely bends over backwards to prevent you from an unplayable game due to debt.  Fall into debt and the game reminds you of the various ways to save money from firing staff to raising prices to taking out a loan.  Once again, you get three different banks with different interest rates and max loans.Fall further, and the game rescues from bankruptcy - but at a cost.  You'll have to choose a couple exhibits to lose to repossession.  Debts to banks are wiped clean and you gain some instant cash, but banks will refuse to lend to you until you reach certain milestones.Building is fairly easy.  The same build engine from Two Point Campus returns, with the ability to save room templates and copy rooms.  You still can't join two buildings on the same plot, but you can demolish the entire museum, send exhibits to storage, and rebuild.And, of course, the beloved world-building of Two Point Radio continues.  DJs Sir Nigel, Ricky, and Harrison return, along with a new hostess, Hayley.  So does the very British humor of the series.  People, items, and locations from the first two games are mentioned or return.Two Point Museum is a solid entry in the series and worth the price of admission.

content: \nWacky Exhibits, Wacky Guests!The hit Two Point County franchise continues with Two Point Museum.  Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.  Everything you love about the franchise returns, including the humor, in-jokes, and Two Point Radio.The game has two modes, Campaign and Sandbox.  Campaign is story-driven and helps introduce various gameplay elements.  Sandbox is essentially the Campaign without the story and allows you to adjust certain parts of the experience before you start.  Thus, Sandbox is best attempted after exploring Campaign mode.You'll have four types of staffers with you.  Experts find exhibits and study and maintain them.  Assistants man the various cash registers - the ticket booths, gift shop, cafeteria, a couple kiosks.  Janitors clean up after litter and vomit and maintain some machinery.  New to the franchise are security guards, needed to watch for criminals as well as securely collect donations.The core gameplay is a cycle of retrieving exhibits and placing and decorating them, as this is what brings in paying guests.Each museum specializes in a theme: Prehistory, Science, Marine Life, Supernatural, Space, with a sixth theme, Botany, secondary in the Prehistory museum.  Exhibits fall into one of the broad themes, and also a subgroup.  Prehistory contains large skeletons as well as smaller fossils, frozen items, and some ancient mysteries.  Botany contains various types of interesting flora.Experts specialize in one of the broad themes.  You send them on expeditions to bring back exhibits via the convenient helicopter parked out back.Each museum gets its own expedition map, but once you unlock locations on other maps, you can freely go to them and pick up exhibits from other themes.  There's also some overlap, as plants are found in several maps and so are dino bones.Each location has specific requirements for expeditions.  First of all, they have to be unlocked, either through the storyline or by reaching certain objectives.  Sandbox mode annoyed me by not carrying over locations unlocked in Campaign to Sandbox.Once unlocked, expeditions to locations have some minimum requirements for the team you send.  Early locations require just one expert.  Later locations ask for two experts, sometimes from different themes, as well as other staffers.  Assistants are like college students helping their professor.  Janitors are needed for their mechanical expertise.  Guards protect valuable cargo.Expeditions are adventurous, and events both good and bad can happen.  This is represented by a few event cards for each location.  Expeditions can find shortcuts or get delayed, or find or lose money.Or something happens to a team member.  Injury, illness, and what the game calls "MIA" can happen.  But the last one is less "missing in action" and more just a polite way of saying "dead," to judge from the events that trigger it and the fact that the unfortunate soul is deleted from your payroll.But not to worry, as there are ways to avoid or mitigate most of the events.  Some bad events happen only at certain times of the year.  Some are cancelled by the total level of your team.Some can be cancelled by cargo items.  Expeditions can carry just one cargo item a trip.  Three are infinite-use, including a first aid kit that takes care of one injury card, but most are one-use items that have to made by a Janitor in a Workshop, such as plant camouflage to sneak past danger.Some locations are one-visit obstructions to clear.  One of the cargo items is a drill to remove pesky rock in the way.Fortunately, none of the events make you lose an exhibit and come away empty-handed.If you're deathly allergic to gacha systems, you'll hate this next part, but it's a very fair gacha system.Locations have one to five different possibilities to find, and exhibits have different rarities.  You will always get one of these, and the "random" roll feels mostly weighted to finding something new.  Even the rarest item can be found in a few trips.Exhibits also have item quality.  Your experts are not fools and know to bring back at least a halfway decent specimen, so the lowest quality is Average.  Top quality is Pristine.There is an easy way and a hard way to get Pristine exhibits.  Easy is to get multi-part exhibits such as large skeletons.  You always find the base first, and pieces to fill it out.  As the exhibit is filled in, quality rises.  A full exhibit instantly becomes Pristine.The hard way, for one-piece exhibits, is by surveying the location.  Each trip gives you more info on a location.  The better a location is surveyed, the easier it is for a team to find that perfect specimen.  You can speed up surveying by going on longer trips and taking a certain cargo item.But you aren't done once you place exhibits, as they have both Buzz and Knowledge.  Buzz excites most guests and is influenced by item quality and the decor around it.  Exhibits also have Buzz Bonuses, a bit of synergy with some piece it wants near it.  Annoyingly, there's different bonuses for different items of the same type and quality exhibit.Knowledge is found by an Expert deconstructing a spare exhibit in an Analysis room, and is displayed on info stands near exhibits.  Some guests, like the Professors, are more excited by Knowledge than Buzz.Criminals cause mischief in your museums.  Vandals just make your Experts and Janitors clean up the place.  Thieves will steal exhibits.  But your security team, including cameras and a guard watching their feeds, can spot them before they strike.  They also have a chance to catch successful thieves and instantly return exhibits.  Thieves who leave the map with an exhibit might eventually ransom it for a premium over sale price.You make money via several sources, ticket sales, cafeteria, gift shop.  You can set prices on most things individually, so you can have cheap tickets and gouge guests at the gift shop, or vice versa.But the main way to gain money is through donations.  Excited guests will happily donate to donation boxes near favorite exhibits.  Security guards collect that money.  This means that money can flow a bit annoyingly inconsistent month to month.Staff wages and item maintenance and ransoms are automatically taken out of your account, so you can fall into negative figures, which prevents you from buying new items, or expeditions or hiring new staff.The game absolutely bends over backwards to prevent you from an unplayable game due to debt.  Fall into debt and the game reminds you of the various ways to save money from firing staff to raising prices to taking out a loan.  Once again, you get three different banks with different interest rates and max loans.Fall further, and the game rescues from bankruptcy - but at a cost.  You'll have to choose a couple exhibits to lose to repossession.  Debts to banks are wiped clean and you gain some instant cash, but banks will refuse to lend to you until you reach certain milestones.Building is fairly easy.  The same build engine from Two Point Campus returns, with the ability to save room templates and copy rooms.  You still can't join two buildings on the same plot, but you can demolish the entire museum, send exhibits to storage, and rebuild.And, of course, the beloved world-building of Two Point Radio continues.  DJs Sir Nigel, Ricky, and Harrison return, along with a new hostess, Hayley.  So does the very British humor of the series.  People, items, and locations from the first two games are mentioned or return.Two Point Museum is a solid entry in the series and worth the price of admission.

content: \nWacky Exhibits, Wacky Guests!The hit Two Point County franchise continues with Two Point Museum.  Manage a museum, acquire and maintaining exhibits for it, fend off thieves, attend to guest needs, and make a profit while you're at it.
